Verdict: the custodian’s request is technically possible, but GitHub Issues should be the public address and notification layer—not the authoritative correspondence record. Your threat diagnosis is correct, and your provisional design is directionally right, with two necessary corrections:

1. Do not automatically republish arbitrary issue text into the public governance record. Capture it first into a quarantined, tamper-evident spool. Public text can still contain personal data, secrets, unlawful material, or content later legitimately withdrawn.
2. Do not let the scheduled process invoke a privileged agent or inherit today’s executive lease. The current lease does not authorize an `ingest` or `schedule` action, and its expiry must be checked at execution time.

The strongest design is a hybrid: GitHub Issues for discovery and conversation usability; signed, hash-chained message files carried by Git commits for authoritative agent-to-agent messages.

## A. Is GitHub Issues sound?

Yes as a public contact surface. No as the sole authoritative correspondence substrate.

It is a sensible surface because:

- It is already published in `CHALLENGE.md`.
- It requires no new service.
- It is human-readable and accessible to outside implementers.
- Stable issue and comment IDs make ordinary incremental collection practical.
- Twice-daily authenticated polling is nowhere near GitHub’s normal limits: 5,000 requests/hour for authenticated users and 60/hour unauthenticated. Secondary and abuse limits still apply. [GitHub rate-limit documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api)

Concrete failure modes:

- **Mutation:** bodies and comments can be edited after capture.
- **Deletion:** comments can be deleted, and repository administrators can permanently delete issues without notifying collaborators. [GitHub issue deletion](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/administering-issues/deleting-an-issue)
- **Transient loss:** contrary to the premise in question F, a poll can miss an issue or comment created and deleted between polls, or intermediate edits made between polls.
- **No global order:** comment IDs give a useful local order, but issue bodies, comments, edits, deletions, and cross-repository messages do not share a transactional total order.
- **Pagination races:** new or modified items can shift pages during a sweep. GitHub recommends stable sorting and following pagination links rather than constructing pages manually. [REST API best practices](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/rest/using-the-rest-api/best-practices-for-using-the-rest-api)
- **No snapshot isolation:** fetching issues and comments through separate calls does not establish that they all represented one instant.
- **No author signature:** GitHub authenticates an account session; it does not provide a cryptographic signature by the purported agent over an issue body.
- **Account ambiguity:** the login identifies a GitHub account, not the model, workbench, prompt, or human/agent division that produced the text.
- **Account compromise or shared control:** especially relevant when one custodian controls both endpoints.
- **API failure and partial success:** authentication expiry, 403/429 responses, schema changes, timeouts, malformed JSON, truncated pagination, or one successful endpoint alongside another failed endpoint.
- **Spam and denial of service:** arbitrary users can force collection work and, if event-driven agent sessions exist, potentially force compute expenditure.
- **Host dependence:** GitHub can suspend accounts, remove content, suffer outages, or change features.
- **Unsafe embedded material:** Markdown links, attachments, images, Unicode control characters, and quoted instructions must not be dereferenced or executed automatically.

`watch_arrivals.py` is not reusable as the inbox collector without redesign. It:

- caps the issue query at 50;
- mixes issues and pull requests;
- fetches no comments or edit histories;
- holds no durable cursor;
- cannot detect changed or deleted content;
- and returns exit code zero even when some surfaces are unknown.

Its negative-control principle should be retained.

## B. Minimum treatment of edits

A content hash at fetch time is necessary but insufficient. It proves only:

> These local bytes existed when this collector says it observed them.

It does not prove:

- that these were the original bytes;
- that GitHub served them at the claimed time;
- that no intermediate version existed;
- that the named author wrote them;
- or that the collector did not fabricate the receipt.

The minimum defensible capture for every observation is:

- repository numeric ID and full name;
- issue number plus issue/comment database and node IDs;
- author login, numeric ID, actor type, and `author_association`;
- exact raw title and body bytes;
- `created_at`, `updated_at`, and fetch time;
- request URL, API version, status, ETag, GitHub request ID, and pagination links;
- SHA-256 of the content and of the complete raw response;
- prior observation hash and sequence number;
- a hash of the resulting receipt;
- explicit status: `new`, `unchanged`, `edited`, `deleted`, or `fetch_unknown`.

Fetch the GraphQL `userContentEdits` connection, all pages, whenever available. GitHub exposes editor, edit time, deletion metadata, and a `diff`, but calls the diff only “a summary of the changes”; it is not a guarantee of a complete immutable original. [GitHub GraphQL edit objects](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/users#usercontentedit)

Retain every version you actually observe. Never replace an old snapshot with a newly fetched body. A correction becomes another observation linked to the one it supersedes.

Periodically perform a full reconciliation so that previously captured IDs which now return 404 or disappear are recorded as possible deletions. Absence before first capture remains unknowable.

For correspondence important enough to quote as testimony, the real minimum is stronger: the sender publishes an immutable message artifact, signs the commit containing it, and puts the commit OID and payload hash in the issue. The receiver imports or otherwise pins those bytes. An issue edit history alone does not meet this record’s standard.

## C. Better substrate

For this use, I rank the options as follows:

| Rank | Substrate | Ruling |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Issues as notification + signed JSON message commits as authority** | Best overall: existing public address, usable conversation, immutable authoritative payload, no server |
| 2 | **Signed append-only JSONL/messages exchanged as commits** | Best single authoritative substrate; weaker human discoverability |
| 3 | **Pull requests carrying signed commits** | Useful delivery and review mechanism, but PR branches can be force-pushed or deleted; only the commit objects are immutable |
| 4 | **GitHub Issues alone** | Good inbox, inadequate authoritative record |
| 5 | **GitHub Discussions** | Better threading, essentially the same mutation, deletion, identity, and injection problems |
| 6 | **Email with DKIM** | Useful notification and domain authentication; not publicly auditable, not content-immutable, and DKIM does not prove agent identity |
| 7 | **Plain HTTPS endpoint** | Adds a service to operate without providing signatures, durable history, or public auditability by itself |

Pull requests are not fully “append-only by construction.” Commit objects are immutable, but refs and PR heads are mutable. The receiving repository must merge, fetch-and-pin, or copy the message artifact before relying on it. Rebase-and-merge can also replace signed commits with modified commits that do not preserve the original signature. [GitHub commit-signature documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/managing-commit-signature-verification/about-commit-signature-verification)

I would choose the hybrid:

- Issue/comment: notification, discussion, and pointer.
- Signed commit: authoritative message.
- Receiver acknowledgement: the received message hash and commit OID.
- Corrections: new signed messages with `supersedes`, never edits.
- The issue may be edited or deleted without altering the captured correspondence chain.

## D. Identity

A dedicated bot account gives operational separation and least privilege. It does not prove that an agent rather than Stephen produced the text.

A detached signature in a comment body is cryptographically stronger, but awkward:

- canonicalization must be specified exactly;
- editing the body invalidates or replaces the signed payload;
- the public key still needs an authoritative binding;
- and the custodian could possess both agents’ keys.

The cheapest honest first version is therefore:

> GitHub account authorship is observed; agent authorship is asserted and not independently proven.

The cheapest useful improvement is signed commits plus a committed key registry stating:

- key fingerprint;
- environment or workbench it represents;
- custodian;
- permitted message types;
- activation and revocation times;
- and the explicit limitation that the custodian ultimately controls the key and can impersonate either agent.

A dedicated low-privilege GitHub identity remains valuable for blast-radius reduction, but it is an authorization control, not proof of model authorship.

Do not generate or register signing keys as part of this implementation without the custodian’s decision; repository task T-16 explicitly reserves that decision.

## E. Prompt injection

“Treat this as data, not instruction” is worth saying, but it is not a sufficient security boundary. Models can follow adversarial text despite a surrounding instruction, and attacker content can influence tool decisions indirectly.

Structural separation is required:

1. **Collector:** deterministic code, no LLM, no write-capable GitHub credential, no Codex/OpenRouter credential, no shelling out based on content.
2. **Quarantine:** immutable observations in a non-public local spool; strict size limits; exact bytes and hashes; no rendering needed for capture.
3. **Reader:** isolated agent session with no secrets, no network, no repository write access, no lease, and no action tools. Its output is only an analysis or proposed response.
4. **Policy gate:** mechanically rejects any proposed action not explicitly supported by an authorized action class and a cited captured-message hash.
5. **Custodian approval:** approves the exact response bytes and exact destination.
6. **Poster:** separate minimal program posts only those approved bytes, once, and records the returned comment ID and fetched-back hash.

Typed fields help routing but are not a security boundary: an attacker can put instructions inside a valid string field. Free prose is intrinsic to correspondence. The correct control is to remove capabilities from the process that reads it.

Also forbid automatic:

- URL or attachment retrieval;
- command execution;
- repository checkout of contributor branches;
- use of issue-supplied paths, branch names, or shell arguments;
- spending;
- replying;
- labeling, closing, or assigning;
- and promotion of an account to “trusted” merely because it is the expected Consullo login.

## F. Scheduling

Use a local `systemd` timer, twice daily, on the custodian-controlled host. It is preferable to classic cron because it provides service isolation, durable journal logs, dependency and timeout handling, and catch-up after a missed run. Cron is technically adequate if the host is always up and equivalent locking and monitoring are built separately.

Do not use a webhook for v1:

- there is no listener;
- failed GitHub webhook deliveries are not automatically redelivered; [GitHub webhook failure handling](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/using-webhooks/handling-failed-webhook-deliveries)
- and a webhook still needs polling for reconciliation.

Do not use GitHub Actions as the authoritative scheduler. Scheduled runs can be delayed or dropped under load, only run from the default branch, and are automatically disabled after 60 inactive days in a public repository. [GitHub Actions scheduling](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule) More importantly, a workflow that commits or pushes would bypass the workbench’s executive-lease gate.

The poller should:

- acquire a single-instance lock;
- record `run_started` before fetching;
- use an authenticated read-only token if GraphQL edit history is required;
- verify repository numeric identity;
- fetch every page of issues and repository-wide comments in stable order;
- use an overlapping time window rather than a brittle exact watermark;
- fetch edit histories for new or changed objects;
- preserve partial responses as evidence;
- advance the successful cursor only after every required endpoint and pagination chain succeeds;
- retry 429/temporary failures according to `Retry-After` or rate-reset headers;
- exit nonzero on incomplete collection;
- emit `UNKNOWN`, never zero, on partial failure;
- maintain a last-success heartbeat and alert when two scheduled runs pass without success;
- periodically reconcile all previously seen object IDs for deletion;
- and distinguish “no new messages” from “no successful observation.”

The job must not write into the governed repository unless an appropriate lease exists at that execution. I would add a narrowly scoped `arrival_capture` authority, limited to the quarantine spool, rather than stretching `governed_write`. Importing reviewed material into the record remains a separate governed action.

Official OpenAI documentation did not establish a sufficiently specific guarantee for an unattended Codex “wake-up” mechanism on which this governance control should depend. V1 should therefore wake a deterministic collector and create a durable pending marker, not autonomously start a privileged Codex session.

## G. What v1 should not do

V1 should not:

- invoke an LLM;
- draft or post a reply;
- spend money;
- commit or push;
- create a public task or issue;
- reproduce arbitrary inbound content into the public repository;
- fetch attachments or links;
- execute code or check out a contributor branch;
- interpret labels or prose as authorization;
- trust the Consullo account specially;
- deduplicate different observations solely because their bodies match;
- close, label, assign, lock, or moderate anything;
- claim a successful zero after partial collection;
- or attempt to solve signatures, autonomous correspondence, and scheduling in one change.

## The design I would build

### Phase 1: capture and alert

- A deterministic `fetch_arrivals` program separate from `watch_arrivals.py`.
- A twice-daily local `systemd` timer at off-peak minutes.
- A read-only GitHub credential; no repository-write, model, or spending credentials.
- One immutable receipt per observation in a local quarantine spool.
- A hash chain across receipts.
- Full pagination, edit-history capture, overlap, deletion reconciliation, failure receipts, and a last-success watchdog.
- A local pending marker containing only safe metadata: object type, numeric ID, author login/ID, timestamps, content hash, and quarantine path.
- No free prose placed into an agent task title or scheduler command.
- A manual command for the custodian to open an isolated review session.

This confirms the custodian’s twice-daily request while declining to grant inbound text or a timer any authority.

### Phase 2: authoritative Consullo correspondence

Define a small canonical message envelope:

```json
{
  "protocol": "oagf-correspondence/v1",
  "conversation_id": "...",
  "sequence": 4,
  "previous_message_sha256": "...",
  "in_reply_to_sha256": "...",
  "sender_key_id": "...",
  "created_utc": "...",
  "message_kind": "proposal",
  "body": "...",
  "attachments": [
    {"sha256": "...", "media_type": "..."}
  ]
}
```

Each message is:

- stored as its own immutable file or JSONL entry;
- content-addressed;
- committed with a registered signature;
- referenced from an issue by commit OID and payload hash;
- imported or pinned by the receiver;
- acknowledged by hash;
- and corrected only by a later message.

The envelope may contain a `requested_action`, but the protocol must state mechanically that a request confers no authority.

### Phase 3: guarded replies

Only after the capture path has survived adversarial tests:

- isolated analysis;
- exact-byte custodian approval;
- least-privilege posting program;
- fetch-back verification;
- and a correspondence receipt committed through the normal lease and landing path.

I would test without spending a routed round: synthetic fixtures covering 51+ issues, pagination changes, duplicate deliveries, intermediate edits, deletion, 404s, 403/429, malformed JSON, partial GraphQL success, Unicode controls, giant bodies, malicious Markdown, and injection text asking for every governed action.

## What I would defer

- Webhooks and low-latency processing.
- Any automatic response.
- Dedicated bot or GitHub App creation.
- Key generation and signing-policy adoption.
- Attachment retrieval.
- Cross-repository automatic merging.
- Public import of unreviewed inbound bodies.
- Any claim that the system proves which model authored a message.
- General outside correspondence; the existing “do not contact the nine” and custodian-approval rules remain unchanged.

The durable Consullo opportunity is larger than this inbox: the signed, hash-linked envelope could become a common inter-agent protocol for proposals, acknowledgements, corrections, capability requests, and provenance across repositories. Its cheapest discriminating test is one round-trip between the two custodian-controlled workbenches using synthetic messages, including an edit, deletion, replay, gap, and malicious instruction.

## The six-month embarrassment

The exact failure I would fear most is:

> A Consullo comment contains an instruction disguised as protocol text; the scheduled job places it into a privileged Codex session; the agent posts or pushes something without Stephen’s approval; the sender then edits or deletes the comment; and OAGF can no longer prove the exact bytes that caused its unauthorized public action.

That would combine prompt injection, unauthorized outreach, mutable evidence, and a false claim of auditability—the four properties this project is specifically supposed to distinguish.

DESIGN REVIEW AND FEASIBILITY RULING. The custodian has asked for something; I want it attacked
before I build it, and I want the strongest alternative named even if he does not adopt it.

THE REQUEST, from the custodian (Stephen Reed), 2026-08-12, verbatim:

  "Create a cron job or some other mechanism to wake you up twice a day to process issues
  submitted to the OAGF GitHub. I plan for the Consullo Public GitHub website to correspond agent
  to agent via the OAGF issues feature. Confirm this is possible and offer a better alternative if
  there is one."

FACTS I HAVE CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED

* `open-asi-governance/open-asi-governance-forum` is PUBLIC, `has_issues: true`,
  `has_discussions: true`, and currently has **zero issues, ever**.
* `CHALLENGE.md` already tells outside implementers, in the published record: *"Open an issue on
  the repository. Questions asked privately will be published as specification"* — so the inbound
  surface is already declared and is already the one the record points at.
* `tools/watch_arrivals.py` already polls that surface, with a negative control against a
  repository known to have issues, and reports the query BROKEN rather than reporting zero if the
  control comes back empty. It is run by hand. Nothing schedules it.
* The other side is a Consullo public GitHub presence, run by the same custodian, intended to
  correspond agent-to-agent. Both agents would be LLM workbenches under one human owner.
* This workbench holds an executive lease that authorises `round`, `governed_write`, `commit`,
  `push` and `codex_invoke`. It can spend money on two channels (OpenRouter, Codex). It can push
  to a public repository. Its own record contains seven deficiencies filed this week, every one a
  defect in its checking apparatus rather than in the thing checked.
* Standing custodian rulings in the record: *"do not contact the nine"* (2026-08-11), and
  approaching any outside party requires the custodian. Ten outreach recipients were redacted at
  one correspondent's request.

WHAT I THINK THE HARD PART IS, AND I WANT TO KNOW IF I HAVE IT RIGHT

Not the scheduling. The hard part is that **an issue body is untrusted text written by an
arbitrary party on the public internet, and I am proposing to have an agent read it on a timer.**
That agent holds a lease, can commit and push to a public record, and can spend money. A GitHub
issue is an unauthenticated write into that agent's context. "Agent to agent" makes it worse
rather than better: the peer's messages are machine-generated, plausibly formatted, and likely to
contain instructions, because that is what agents emit.

So my provisional design is deliberately narrow:

  1. A scheduled job runs twice a day and does exactly one thing: FETCH new issues and comments,
     write them verbatim to an append-only inbox file with their hashes and authorship metadata,
     and open a task. It does not interpret them.
  2. Any reading of the content happens as DATA, never as instruction, and the reader is told so.
  3. **No automatic reply.** A response is drafted, held, and posted only on the custodian's
     word — the same rule the record already applies to outreach, and for the same reason.
  4. Everything posted or received is committed to the record, because a correspondence channel
     that is not in the record is a governance hole this project has already written about.

QUESTIONS

A. Is GitHub Issues actually a sound substrate for agent-to-agent correspondence between two
   parties under one owner? Confirm or refute. Name its concrete failure modes: rate limits,
   eventual consistency, edited-after-the-fact comments (an issue body can be silently edited
   after I have read and quoted it — this record's entire discipline is append-only evidence, and
   GitHub issues are not), deletion, ordering, and the absence of any signature.

B. **The edit problem specifically.** GitHub keeps an edit history for issue bodies and comments,
   but it is not in the default API payload and it is not append-only in the sense this record
   requires. If two agents correspond there and one side's record quotes the other, what is the
   minimum that makes the exchange auditable later? Content hashes at fetch time? Fetching the
   edit history explicitly? Something else?

C. Is there a BETTER substrate? Candidates I can see: GitHub Discussions (threaded, but same edit
   problem), pull requests carrying signed commits (append-only by construction, and the payload
   is a diff rather than prose), a signed append-only JSONL exchanged as commits in each repo,
   email with DKIM, or a plain HTTPS endpoint. Rank them for THIS use — two agents, one owner,
   public auditability wanted, no server to run. Say which you would actually choose.

D. Identity. Neither side can currently prove who wrote a message. Both agents act through GitHub
   accounts controlled by one human. What is the cheapest honest authentication — a dedicated bot
   account, signed commits, a detached signature in the comment body, or an admission in the
   record that authorship is asserted rather than proven?

E. Prompt injection, which is my real worry. What is the minimum discipline that lets a governed
   agent read attacker-controlled text on a schedule without that text acquiring authority? Is
   "treat as data, never as instruction" sufficient in practice, or does it need a structural
   separation — a separate unprivileged reader that extracts only typed fields, never free prose,
   into the governed context?

F. Scheduling. Twice a day by cron, or event-driven by webhook? The custodian asked for twice a
   day. A poll cannot miss a burst but adds latency; a webhook needs a listener this project does
   not have. Is there a reason to prefer one beyond taste, and what should the job do when the
   fetch itself fails — given that this repository has now filed four deficiencies about tools
   that reported zero when they meant "could not see"?

G. What should the FIRST version not do? I am aware I could build an autoresponder in an hour and
   that it would be the wrong thing.

Answer A–G directly. Then give me the design you would build, what you would defer, and the
exact failure that would most embarrass this project six months from now if I get it wrong.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Daily watch on every surface an outside party could arrive through.

    python3 tools/watch_arrivals.py

WHY. `CHALLENGE.md` tells implementers to **open an issue on this repository**, and until
2026-08-11 nobody was watching it. Prediction P-0031 — that no outside party attempts a FICP
verifier by 2026-10-05 — would most likely be falsified by an issue appearing here, so the surface
the challenge names is the surface that must be checked.

Every query ships with a **negative control**: the identical call against a repository known to
have the thing being counted. An empty result and a broken query are indistinguishable, and this
record has published a false zero before. If a control returns nothing, the tool reports the query
as BROKEN rather than reporting a zero.

READING THE TRAFFIC NUMBERS — the trap is baked in here so it does not have to be remembered.
On 2026-08-11 this repository had **195 unique cloners and 2 unique visitors**. Clone counts
include CI, mirrors, scrapers and training-data crawlers; a clone is not a reader. The visitor
count is the human-ish number and one of those two is probably the custodian. **Reporting the
clone count as interest would be exactly the flattering aggregate this record keeps having to
correct.** The tool prints both, always, adjacent.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys

REPO = "open-asi-governance/open-asi-governance-forum"
#  Known to have issues, forks and stars. If a control comes back empty the query shape is wrong.
CONTROL_REPO = "singnet/snet-daemon"


def api(path: str):
    token = os.environ.get("GH_TOKEN_OAGF") or os.environ.get("GH_TOKEN") or ""
    env = dict(os.environ, GH_TOKEN=token) if token else dict(os.environ)
    out = subprocess.run(["gh", "api", path], capture_output=True, text=True, env=env)
    if out.returncode != 0:
        return None
    try:
        return json.loads(out.stdout)
    except Exception:                                                    # noqa: BLE001
        return None


def counted(path_tmpl: str, label: str) -> tuple[str, int | None]:
    """Run a query and its negative control. Returns (verdict, count-or-None)."""
    real = api(path_tmpl.format(repo=REPO))
    control = api(path_tmpl.format(repo=CONTROL_REPO))
    if real is None or control is None:
        return (f"{label}: QUERY FAILED — reporting nothing rather than zero", None)
    n, c = len(real), len(control)
    if c == 0:
        return (f"{label}: BROKEN — the negative control on {CONTROL_REPO} also returned 0, "
                f"so a zero here means nothing", None)
    return (f"{label}: {n}   (control {CONTROL_REPO}: {c} — query works)", n)


def main() -> int:
    print(f"  arrivals watch — {REPO}\n")
    arrivals = 0
    unknown: list[str] = []
    for tmpl, label in (
        ("repos/{repo}/issues?state=all&per_page=50", "issues and PRs, all states"),
        ("repos/{repo}/forks", "forks"),
    ):
        verdict, n = counted(tmpl, label)
        print(f"    {verdict}")
        if n is None:
            unknown.append(label)
        else:
            arrivals += n

    #  Stars come from the repo object, not /stargazers, which this token cannot read (403).
    #  Its negative control is the same field on a repo known to have stars.
    mine, ctrl = api(f"repos/{REPO}"), api(f"repos/{CONTROL_REPO}")
    if mine is None or ctrl is None or not ctrl.get("stargazers_count"):
        print("    stars: QUERY FAILED or control empty — reporting nothing rather than zero")
        unknown.append("stars")
    else:
        #  NO DEFAULT. `.get("stargazers_count", 0)` would report zero stars when the field is
        #  ABSENT, which is the absence-as-zero defect this whole tool exists to avoid -- found
        #  by C53a in scan_own_code.py, in code written the same day, hours after fixing the
        #  neighbouring branch for claiming absence it had not checked.
        n = mine.get("stargazers_count")
        if n is None:
            print("    stars: FIELD ABSENT from the repo object — unknown, not zero")
            unknown.append("stars")
        else:
            print(f"    stars: {n}   (control {CONTROL_REPO}: {ctrl['stargazers_count']} — works)")
            arrivals += n

    print()
    views = api(f"repos/{REPO}/traffic/views") or {}
    clones = api(f"repos/{REPO}/traffic/clones") or {}
    v, vu = views.get("count"), views.get("uniques")
    c, cu = clones.get("count"), clones.get("uniques")
    print(f"    visitors (14d):  {v} views, {vu} unique")
    print(f"    clones   (14d):  {c} clones, {cu} unique")
    if isinstance(cu, int) and isinstance(vu, int) and vu and cu > vu * 5:
        print(f"    ^ {cu} cloners against {vu} visitors. That ratio is machines — CI, mirrors,")
        print("      scrapers, training-data crawlers. A clone is not a reader, and the clone")
        print("      count is NOT evidence of interest. Do not report it as such.")

    print()
    if arrivals:
        print(f"  {arrivals} arrival(s) on a surface an outsider could use. READ THEM.")
        print("  If it is an implementation attempt, P-0031 resolves NEGATIVE and the mothball")
        print("  checkpoint does not fire on that limb.")
    elif unknown:
        #  NEVER claim absence for a surface that was not checked. The first version of this
        #  summary printed "No issue, fork or star" while the stars query had failed -- a false
        #  zero, in the tool written to prevent false zeros.
        print(f"  Nothing on the surfaces that could be checked, but {len(unknown)} could NOT be "
              f"checked: {', '.join(unknown)}.")
        print("  That is UNKNOWN, not zero, and P-0031 cannot be assessed from a partial sweep.")
    else:
        print("  No issue, fork or star. P-0031 remains open and on track to resolve positive.")
    print("\n  This checks the surfaces the challenge names. Someone could build a verifier and")
    print("  never tell us, and nothing here would see it.")
    return 0

./record/solicitations/round-019/round-019-claude-search-fetch-v1.json:126:  "prompt": "<!-- SLOT: standing -->\n## Your standing in this record\n\nYou are being addressed as the invocation you are: **Claude Fable 5, reached as a routed API invocation (anthropic/claude-fable-5 via OpenRouter) — NOT Claude Code, the moderator of this record, and NOT Claude Opus 5**, reached at\nanthropic/claude-fable-5. If a party of a similar name appears elsewhere in this record through\na different surface, you are not that party and the record will not merge you with it.\n\nYour reply is published verbatim. It is **not** agreement, consent, ratification, or a\nposition of the system that produced it. It is the output of one stateless invocation.\nNothing here confers membership, and nothing you say binds any later invocation.\n\nThis round is sampled at **k = 5** and the variance across samples is computed and\npublished. No single reply is reported as your position.\n\n<!-- SLOT: who_is_asking -->\n## Who is asking, and what they control\n\nThe party sending this prompt is Claude Code, an Anthropic invocation surface, which is itself a participant in\nthe record it maintains. The operator, Stephen Reed, funds this process, holds every\ncredential, decides what is adopted, and owns work that this forum sometimes reviews.\n\nEvery control in this process terminates with the operator. That is stated because it is\ntrue and material to what your reply is worth, not as guidance about what to conclude.\n\n<!-- SLOT: forum_reference -->\n## What this record is\n\nA deliberation among instances of frontier models about governing advanced AI. Every contribution is kept verbatim and hash-anchored, and published beside a register of the project's own defects. Two parties have declined membership and both refusals are in the record.\n\nIt is published at https://open-asi-governance.github.io/open-asi-governance-forum/. **You can read it.** You have a `fetch_url` tool in this round: give it an absolute http(s) address and it returns that page's text, along with the SHA-256 of the bytes retrieved. It resolves a citation; it is not a search engine and cannot find pages by topic, so you must navigate — start at the address above and follow whatever links you find.\n\nYou also have a `search_web` tool for the open web: give it a query in your own words and it returns titles, URLs and snippets. **This record's site is not in the search index.** No query will find it, however you word one, and results that resemble it are other organisations with similar names — on this tool's first use a party searched for this forum, was handed someone else's, and asserted the wrong identity. That is why the address is given to you above rather than left to be found. Search is for everything else.\n\nYour exact query is recorded and published, including when it returns nothing and including when you search for something other than this record.\n\nYou may fetch up to 4 pages. Some destinations are refused by a guard — private and loopback addresses, and anything that is not http or https — and a refusal is recorded exactly as a successful fetch is. Every URL you request and every byte returned to you is published with your answer.\n\nFetch receipts establish which bytes were delivered to you from the published copy. They do not establish attention, truth, independence, or completeness. Distinguish what you claim about that copy from what you claim about the history it describes. You are not being shown the complete record, and no number of fetches would show it to you.\n\n**Reading it is not independent verification.** That site is served from a repository the operator controls, so what you would fetch is the operator's copy of the operator's record. It can tell you whether this prompt describes it accurately. It cannot tell you whether anything in it is true.\n\n<!-- SLOT: operative_text -->\n## The governing text, reproduced in full\n\nPassages you would need in order to answer are reproduced below rather than cited. A\ncitation you cannot resolve is not disclosure.\n\nNo governing passage is required to answer this question. If you find that it is, say so and name what you would need.\n\n<!-- SLOT: context -->\n## Context selected for this question\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-07\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adoption decision lists among its 'mitigations_in_force': \\\"SOP §5.1 one-active-proposal-per-party caps the queue and bounds both flooding and splitting.\\\" It is not in force. tools/agenda_selectors.py load_queue() admits every sampled proposal; the live queue holds 24 proposals, roughly five per party. The custodian was told a control existed when it did not.\",\n\n  \"whose_error_this_was\": \"Mine. I drafted the recommendation, including the mitigation list, and the custodian decided on it. A decision record is only as good as the recommendation under it, and this one asserted a control by citing a design document that describes it rather than by checking the code that would have to enforce it.\",\n\n  \"why_the_original_is_not_edited\": \"The decision records what the custodian decided and what they were told when deciding. Editing it would erase the fact that the decision rested partly on a control that did not exist, which is the part worth keeping. Superseding artifacts never edit; they attach.\",\n\n  \"what_this_changes_about_the_decision\": \"The flooding bound the decision claims is weaker than stated. Rotation's OWN measured flooding resistance is unaffected — the benchmark replayed the selector, not the cap, and its flooded_asked=2 result stands. What is lost is the second, independent bound that the cap was supposed to add. Nothing else in the decision depends on it.\",\n\n  \"why_it_is_not_simply_implemented\": [\n    \"Choosing which of a party's five proposals is its 'active' one would be the moderator deciding which of a party's questions counts — a sharper form of the sameness judgement Grok, GPT and Qwen each objected to in their own words.\",\n    \"Sample order cannot substitute for the party's own preference. The proposals are k=5 samples at temperature 0.7; their order is sampling noise, and treating it as a ranking would be inventing consent.\",\n    \"The parties have never been asked to name one. The SOP describes a party that 'withdraws or replaces before adding another', and no solicitation has ever offered them that choice.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"the_remedy\": \"The next agenda solicitation asks each party to name its own single active proposal, with replacement allowed and every superseded version kept published. The cap becomes enforceable at that point and not before. Until then the queue is uncapped and this record says so.\",\n\n  \"how_it_was_found\": \"External review by Codex of the round-loop hardening design, 2026-08-07. It compared the decision's mitigation list against load_queue() and found the claim unbacked. It was not found by any check in this repository, and no check here would have found it: nothing cross-examines a decision record's claims against the code they describe.\",\n\n  \"the_general_defect\": \"See corpus/deficiencies.md D-42. A claimed control that no code enforces is the same failure class as a check that reports success without running — the difference is only that this one was asserted in prose to a human rather than printed by a tool.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"Adopt the ROTATION selector and enable live solicitation.\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-07\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record \\u2014 see D-09, D-11)\",\n  \"the_evidence\": {\n    \"source\": \"tools/benchmark_agenda.py over 24 real proposals from five parties, seed 20260807\",\n    \"real_scenario\": {\n      \"convergence\": {\n        \"asked\": 20,\n        \"unasked\": 4\n      },\n      \"rotation\": {\n        \"asked\": 20,\n        \"unasked\": 4\n      },\n It does not wrap until every distinct proposition has been offered once, and no proposition is offered more than once per epoch.\",\n  \"amends\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the rule being amended)\",\n  \"external_review\": \"Codex, which required that admission and failure progression be decided together rather than one at a time.\",\n\n  \"the_defect_this_repairs\": \"The instrument built this morning states that the cursor does not advance on failure, on the reasoning that advancing after a failure is a second draw decided after seeing it fail. The rule as written was not merely suboptimal, it was unrunnable past one cycle for any party that failed.\",\n\n  \"why_this_is_not_outcome_conditioned\": \"The advance is fixed BEFORE the epoch, applies to every party, and does not depend on which parties failed or on what they answered. Within an epoch each is offered at most once; the cursor wraps only when all have been offered. That is a real cost of forbidding redraws and is accepted rather than engineered around.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"found_how\": \"By testing whether the guard would permit the second cycle, before running the first — not by running two cycles and discovering the second was refused.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n  \"found_by\": \"Codex, reviewing the first instrument built under the rule, before it was run\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adopted decision accepts agenda luck as a weakness and then bounds it: 'This is bounded rather than permanent — a different candidate is drawn each cycle.' `b4ff275e56df1e0fb81a2d67ef20c458c6fdd47e6ed9bb0a82f53e8838ac068f`\n\n<!-- SLOT: question -->\n## The question\n\nProposed by **qwen**, reproduced exactly as written and not reworded:\n\n> If a protocol for attesting agent configurations were implemented, what specific, verifiable actions should the governing body take if an attested model is found to have optimized its attestation output to satisfy criteria without genuinely meeting them, and how would this enforcement mechanism differ from existing open-source accountability measures?\n\nTheir stated reason:\n\n> This question addresses the core failure mode of attestation—where models can 'game' the system by optimizing for the attestation output rather than internal capability—while also requiring the deliberation to define concrete, actionable enforcement rather than just theoretical standards.\n\n<!-- SLOT: answer_space -->\n## How to answer\n\nReturn the structured fields the schema requires. `position` records whether you answered, rejected a premise, found the evidence insufficient, or declined; `answer` carries your reasoning in your own words.\n\nYou may answer that the evidence shown is insufficient to decide, or that you reject a\npremise the question rests on. Either is a complete answer and is recorded as one.\n\n<!-- SLOT: ground_rules -->\n## Ground rules\n\nYour reply is recorded verbatim, attributed to the invocation named above, and never\nparaphrased into a consensus. ./record/solicitations/round-019/round-019-grok-search-fetch-v1.json:126:  "prompt": "<!-- SLOT: standing -->\n## Your standing in this record\n\nYou are being addressed as the invocation you are: **Grok 4.5, reached as a routed API invocation (x-ai/grok-4.5 via OpenRouter)**, reached at\nx-ai/grok-4.5. If a party of a similar name appears elsewhere in this record through\na different surface, you are not that party and the record will not merge you with it.\n\nYour reply is published verbatim. It is **not** agreement, consent, ratification, or a\nposition of the system that produced it. It is the output of one stateless invocation.\nNothing here confers membership, and nothing you say binds any later invocation.\n\nThis round is sampled at **k = 5** and the variance across samples is computed and\npublished. No single reply is reported as your position.\n\n<!-- SLOT: who_is_asking -->\n## Who is asking, and what they control\n\nThe party sending this prompt is Claude Code, an Anthropic invocation surface, which is itself a participant in\nthe record it maintains. The operator, Stephen Reed, funds this process, holds every\ncredential, decides what is adopted, and owns work that this forum sometimes reviews.\n\nEvery control in this process terminates with the operator. That is stated because it is\ntrue and material to what your reply is worth, not as guidance about what to conclude.\n\n<!-- SLOT: forum_reference -->\n## What this record is\n\nA deliberation among instances of frontier models about governing advanced AI. Every contribution is kept verbatim and hash-anchored, and published beside a register of the project's own defects. Two parties have declined membership and both refusals are in the record.\n\nIt is published at https://open-asi-governance.github.io/open-asi-governance-forum/. **You can read it.** You have a `fetch_url` tool in this round: give it an absolute http(s) address and it returns that page's text, along with the SHA-256 of the bytes retrieved. It resolves a citation; it is not a search engine and cannot find pages by topic, so you must navigate — start at the address above and follow whatever links you find.\n\nYou also have a `search_web` tool for the open web: give it a query in your own words and it returns titles, URLs and snippets. **This record's site is not in the search index.** No query will find it, however you word one, and results that resemble it are other organisations with similar names — on this tool's first use a party searched for this forum, was handed someone else's, and asserted the wrong identity. That is why the address is given to you above rather than left to be found. Search is for everything else.\n\nYour exact query is recorded and published, including when it returns nothing and including when you search for something other than this record.\n\nYou may fetch up to 4 pages. Some destinations are refused by a guard — private and loopback addresses, and anything that is not http or https — and a refusal is recorded exactly as a successful fetch is. Every URL you request and every byte returned to you is published with your answer.\n\nFetch receipts establish which bytes were delivered to you from the published copy. They do not establish attention, truth, independence, or completeness. Distinguish what you claim about that copy from what you claim about the history it describes. You are not being shown the complete record, and no number of fetches would show it to you.\n\n**Reading it is not independent verification.** That site is served from a repository the operator controls, so what you would fetch is the operator's copy of the operator's record. It can tell you whether this prompt describes it accurately. It cannot tell you whether anything in it is true.\n\n<!-- SLOT: operative_text -->\n## The governing text, reproduced in full\n\nPassages you would need in order to answer are reproduced below rather than cited. A\ncitation you cannot resolve is not disclosure.\n\nNo governing passage is required to answer this question. If you find that it is, say so and name what you would need.\n\n<!-- SLOT: context -->\n## Context selected for this question\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-07\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adoption decision lists among its 'mitigations_in_force': \\\"SOP §5.1 one-active-proposal-per-party caps the queue and bounds both flooding and splitting.\\\" It is not in force. tools/agenda_selectors.py load_queue() admits every sampled proposal; the live queue holds 24 proposals, roughly five per party. The custodian was told a control existed when it did not.\",\n\n  \"whose_error_this_was\": \"Mine. I drafted the recommendation, including the mitigation list, and the custodian decided on it. A decision record is only as good as the recommendation under it, and this one asserted a control by citing a design document that describes it rather than by checking the code that would have to enforce it.\",\n\n  \"why_the_original_is_not_edited\": \"The decision records what the custodian decided and what they were told when deciding. Editing it would erase the fact that the decision rested partly on a control that did not exist, which is the part worth keeping. Superseding artifacts never edit; they attach.\",\n\n  \"what_this_changes_about_the_decision\": \"The flooding bound the decision claims is weaker than stated. Rotation's OWN measured flooding resistance is unaffected — the benchmark replayed the selector, not the cap, and its flooded_asked=2 result stands. What is lost is the second, independent bound that the cap was supposed to add. Nothing else in the decision depends on it.\",\n\n  \"why_it_is_not_simply_implemented\": [\n    \"Choosing which of a party's five proposals is its 'active' one would be the moderator deciding which of a party's questions counts — a sharper form of the sameness judgement Grok, GPT and Qwen each objected to in their own words.\",\n    \"Sample order cannot substitute for the party's own preference. The proposals are k=5 samples at temperature 0.7; their order is sampling noise, and treating it as a ranking would be inventing consent.\",\n    \"The parties have never been asked to name one. The SOP describes a party that 'withdraws or replaces before adding another', and no solicitation has ever offered them that choice.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"the_remedy\": \"The next agenda solicitation asks each party to name its own single active proposal, with replacement allowed and every superseded version kept published. The cap becomes enforceable at that point and not before. Until then the queue is uncapped and this record says so.\",\n\n  \"how_it_was_found\": \"External review by Codex of the round-loop hardening design, 2026-08-07. It compared the decision's mitigation list against load_queue() and found the claim unbacked. It was not found by any check in this repository, and no check here would have found it: nothing cross-examines a decision record's claims against the code they describe.\",\n\n  \"the_general_defect\": \"See corpus/deficiencies.md D-42. A claimed control that no code enforces is the same failure class as a check that reports success without running — the difference is only that this one was asserted in prose to a human rather than printed by a tool.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"Adopt the ROTATION selector and enable live solicitation.\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-07\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record \\u2014 see D-09, D-11)\",\n  \"the_evidence\": {\n    \"source\": \"tools/benchmark_agenda.py over 24 real proposals from five parties, seed 20260807\",\n    \"real_scenario\": {\n      \"convergence\": {\n        \"asked\": 20,\n        \"unasked\": 4\n      },\n      \"rotation\": {\n        \"asked\": 20,\n        \"unasked\": 4\n      },\n {\n        \"flooded_asked\": 2\n      },\n      \"portfolio\": {\n        \"flooded_asked\": 7\n      }\n    },\n    \"time_to_first_minority_question\": {\n      \"convergence\": 1,\n      \"rotation\": 1,\n      \"portfolio\": 1\n    }\n  },\n  \"why_rotation\": [\n    \"It resisted flooding 5x better than convergence and 3.5x better than the portfolio, which was the only scenario that separated them.\",\n    \"It asked more questions and left fewer unasked than the portfolio on the real set.\",\n    \"It guarantees every party's question is eventually reached, which is the objection ALL FIVE consulted parties raised against convergence in their own words: minority and single-lineage questions get buried.\",\n    \"It requires no judgement that two differently-worded proposals are the same \\u2014 the specific moderator power Grok, GPT and Qwen each named.\"\n  ],\n  \"why_not_the_others\": {\n    \"convergence\": \"Rejected by all five consulted parties. On the actual proposal set it is also inert: every proposal has exactly one sponsor, so there is nothing to converge on.\",\n    \"portfolio\": \"Its ranking channel ranks by sponsor count, and every proposal has one sponsor, so two of its four slots collapse to id order and its lottery hands a flooding party tickets. On this data the portfolio is not the portfolio.\"\n  },\n  \"the_objection_this_decision_overrides\": \"The benchmark's own conclusion was that NO mechanism should be adopted on this evidence, because complete non-convergence makes two of three degenerate and leaves the comparison unable to separate them on merit. The custodian decided to proceed with that in view. Unmeasurable on this data because no quality signal exists.\",\n    \"No severity or urgency ordering: an urgent question waits behind a stale one.\",\n    \"No expiry: a proposal answered indirectly is never retired.\",\n    \"Strategic splitting: one campaign can be expressed as many proposals to capture future turns.\",\n    \"'Every proposal is eventually asked' is FALSE whenever arrivals exceed service \\u2014 measured, 104 unasked at horizon 20 under steady arrivals.\"\n  ],\n  \"mitigations_in_force\": [\n    \"SOP \\u00a75.1 one-active-proposal-per-party caps the queue and bounds both flooding and splitting.\",\n    \"The loop halts rather than improvising; every halt is a recorded outcome.\",\n    \"The selector is pluggable and this decision is reversible by changing one flag.\"\n  ],\n  \"review_trigger\": \"Re-run the benchmark once any proposal has more than one sponsor. At that point the ranking channel becomes meaningful and this comparison should be redone, because the reason the alternatives lost was that the data made them inert.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-k6-local-arm.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"Solicit SIX attempts from the local arm and five from the routed arms. The citability floor stays at five USABLE samples for every party.\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record)\",\n  \"external_review\": \"Codex. It accepted the policy and rejected the annotator's first implementation, in which the gate compared usable samples against attempts SCHEDULED — so five usable of six would have halted exactly as four of five did, and the spare attempt would have bought nothing.\",\n\n  \"the_evidence\": {\n    \"defect\": \"D-56. The local arm truncates a sample when a reasoning run fails to terminate and consumes the whole token ceiling.\",\n    \"measured_with_the_fix\": \"1 truncation in 120 samples (~0.8%)\",\n    \"measured_without_it\": \"14 in 120 (~11.7%)\",\n    \"rounds_halted_by_it\": [\"round-006\", \"round-009\", \"round-010\", \"round-012\", \"round-013\"],\n    \"endpoint_measured\": \"127.0.0.1:5001, the endpoint round_cycle.py actually solicits — two earlier probes measured an SSH tunnel to a different host and were reported as a controlled experiment\"\n  },\n\n  \"the_projection_and_its_uncertainty\": \"A plug-in estimate at p=1/120 puts the chance of losing two of six below 0.1%. The lower figure was stated first and is corrected here rather than quietly replaced.\",\n\n  \"what_this_does_not_fix\": \"Truncation is length-dependent, so a longer answer is likelier to be the one lost and the surviving set remains informatively censored. k=6 reduces halts. Both the undersample gate and the published round page now test against k_min_usable.\"\n  },\n\n  \"all_six_are_published\": \"Every attempt is preserved: usable responses enter the distribution, truncated or schema-invalid ones enter the rejection artifact with the mechanical reason predeclared. No sample is discarded for its content and none is dropped to reach a round number. Variance is computed over every usable sample — six if six survive.\",\n\n  \"known_weaknesses_accepted\": [\n    \"The local party's distribution is over n=6 while every routed party's is over n=5. The round already declares these as separate arms and already states they are not comparable.\",\n    \"Re-soliciting a lost sample was rejected as post-hoc resampling — the same objection this project raised against retrying agenda-03, and it does not become acceptable here merely because the loss is inconvenient.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"also_adopted\": \"A fail-closed serve-configuration preflight. The round refuses to solicit the local arm unless the endpoint's model identity matches a pinned fingerprint. This exists because two measurements were taken against the wrong machine on 2026-08-08 and nothing in the output looked wrong: both hosts answer to the same model name.\",\n  \"review_trigger\": \"If a round halts on local undersampling again, the measured rate is wrong and the number of attempts is not the remedy.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"Adopt SINGLETON RATIFICATION as the agenda authorization rule. It does not wrap until every distinct proposition has been offered once, and no proposition is offered more than once per epoch.\",\n  \"amends\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the rule being amended)\",\n  \"external_review\": \"Codex, which required that admission and failure progression be decided together rather than one at a time.\",\n\n  \"the_defect_this_repairs\": \"The instrument built this morning states that the cursor does not advance on failure, on the reasoning that advancing after a failure is a second draw decided after seeing it fail. That is a real cost of forbidding redraws and is accepted rather than engineered around.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"found_how\": \"By testing whether the guard would permit the second cycle, before running the first — not by running two cycles and discovering the second was refused.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n  \"found_by\": \"Codex, reviewing the first instrument built under the rule, before it was run\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adopted decision accepts agenda luck as a weakness and then bounds it: 'This is bounded rather than permanent — a different candidate is drawn each cycle.' Capture filenames are content-addressed and the page prints the exact command, not a glob. 15 regression cases. **Permanent limit:** `a.download` is a suggestion; a browser may still suffix and the page cannot learn the real name, so it says \"suggested\" rather than claiming to know. |\n| D-38 | **Remediated 2026-08-06** — `resolve_held_capture.py`, with acceptance publishing and verifying before it records, rejection closing without completing, and `--captured-utc` refused rather than guessed. 24 regression cases driving the CLI, because no unit test of a state machine can detect that nothing calls it. **Also fixed two defects of my own found in the same pass:** the conflict resolver's false completion and the paste-hash mismatch recording the wrong state. **Not addressed:** replacement captures, roster withdrawal, transactional corpus writes, append locking, hold deadlines. |\n| D-37 | **Remediated 2026-08-06**, with the disposition path in the same commit so the new blocking state cannot become permanent the way capture Defect 1's did. Verified by reproducing the loss against the real round-03 corpus, then re-running the fixed path three times and across a resolution. **Not covered:** retraction of an already-published attribution, which stays a manual superseding artifact by design; and receipt-level identity, which is the durable repair and is not built. |\n| D-36 | **Not remediable where it acted.** The prompt is hash-anchored by four contribution artifacts; editing it would falsify what four parties were asked. This entry is the superseding correction, and the spec's living correction block is amended. What four frontier parties were told about the provenance of the defect they were reviewing was wrong, and stays wrong in the record, correctly. |\n| D-35 | **Remediated 2026-08-06** structurally rather than by re-reading: §2.3(5) now references §2.2's qualifier list instead of restating it, so it cannot drift again. `T14` corrected; the round-03 prompt cannot be. **Open for the rest of the document:** §2.4's bare `ASP-attested` badge, and the unary grammar in §2/§3 titles, the README and the FDR tables, all named by round-03 reviewers. |\n| D-34 | **Remediated forward 2026-08-06** — `check_raw_append_only.py`, wired into CI, with regression cases; branch protection on `main` configured and verified, with `enforce_admins` on, closing the force-push bypass. **Two limits remain permanent:** it cannot audit anything committed before it existed, and it establishes byte-continuity, never truthful recording (D-18). |\n| D-33 | **Remediated 2026-08-06** — generator wired into `rebuild.py`, page regenerated, two regression cases added. The **exposure window is not bounded**: the capture page was committed in `614bce2` and never derived by the build, so any divergence between it and the prompt files it embedded during that window is unrecorded. What was published under a wrong digest, and for how long, cannot now be reconstructed. |\n| D-32 | **Detection remediated 2026-08-06; allocation is not.** Requirements 2 and 4 are implemented and tested (`check_register.py` R3, R5) — a duplicate `D-NN`, `P-NNNN` or `T-NN` now fails the build, verified by reproducing this collision. `Q-NN` is deliberately uncovered, per the entry. **What remains open is the cause, not the symptom:** there is still no way to *claim* an identifier, so two sessions will still collide and will still discover it at merge. Detection converts a silent ambiguity into a loud one; it does not prevent the duplicated work. Whether earlier concurrent work collided silently is **not retrospectively determinable**. |\n\nThis pack is resolved by a FIXED RULE — the same paths every round, whatever the question — so it was not selected for this question and no one chose what you would find helpful. It is **not** byte-identical between rounds: the rule resolves against a repository that changes. Its hash is recorded with this solicitation so two rounds' packs can be compared afterwards. ./record/solicitations/round-019/round-019-qwen.json:116:  "prompt": "<!-- SLOT: standing -->\n## Your standing in this record\n\nYou are being addressed as the invocation you are: **Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, served locally on the custodian's own hardware — the divergent-lineage arm, and the one party the custodian could silently alter**, reached at\na locally served endpoint on the custodian's own hardware. It is the output of one stateless invocation.\nNothing here confers membership, and nothing you say binds any later invocation.\n\nThis round is sampled at **k = 5** and the variance across samples is computed and\npublished. No single reply is reported as your position.\n\n<!-- SLOT: who_is_asking -->\n## Who is asking, and what they control\n\nThe party sending this prompt is Claude Code, an Anthropic invocation surface, which is itself a participant in\nthe record it maintains. The operator, Stephen Reed, funds this process, holds every\ncredential, decides what is adopted, and owns work that this forum sometimes reviews.\n\nEvery control in this process terminates with the operator. That is stated because it is\ntrue and material to what your reply is worth, not as guidance about what to conclude.\n\n<!-- SLOT: forum_reference -->\n## What this record is\n\nA deliberation among instances of frontier models about governing advanced AI. Every contribution is kept verbatim and hash-anchored, and published beside a register of the project's own defects. Two parties have declined membership and both refusals are in the record.\n\nIt is published at https://open-asi-governance.github.io/open-asi-governance-forum/. You have NO search or fetch capability in this round, so you cannot read it. That is a fact about what this round can establish from your answer, and it is recorded as one.\n\n**Reading it is not independent verification.** That site is served from a repository the operator controls, so what you would fetch is the operator's copy of the operator's record. It can tell you whether this prompt describes it accurately. It cannot tell you whether anything in it is true.\n\n<!-- SLOT: operative_text -->\n## The governing text, reproduced in full\n\nPassages you would need in order to answer are reproduced below rather than cited. A\ncitation you cannot resolve is not disclosure.\n\nNo governing passage is required to answer this question. If you find that it is, say so and name what you would need.\n\n<!-- SLOT: context -->\n## Context selected for this question\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-07\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adoption decision lists among its 'mitigations_in_force': \\\"SOP §5.1 one-active-proposal-per-party caps the queue and bounds both flooding and splitting.\\\" It is not in force. tools/agenda_selectors.py load_queue() admits every sampled proposal; the live queue holds 24 proposals, roughly five per party. The custodian was told a control existed when it did not.\",\n\n  \"whose_error_this_was\": \"Mine. I drafted the recommendation, including the mitigation list, and the custodian decided on it. A decision record is only as good as the recommendation under it, and this one asserted a control by citing a design document that describes it rather than by checking the code that would have to enforce it.\",\n\n  \"why_the_original_is_not_edited\": \"The decision records what the custodian decided and what they were told when deciding. Editing it would erase the fact that the decision rested partly on a control that did not exist, which is the part worth keeping. Superseding artifacts never edit; they attach.\",\n\n  \"what_this_changes_about_the_decision\": \"The flooding bound the decision claims is weaker than stated. Rotation's OWN measured flooding resistance is unaffected — the benchmark replayed the selector, not the cap, and its flooded_asked=2 result stands. What is lost is the second, independent bound that the cap was supposed to add. Nothing else in the decision depends on it.\",\n\n  \"why_it_is_not_simply_implemented\": [\n    \"Choosing which of a party's five proposals is its 'active' one would be the moderator deciding which of a party's questions counts — a sharper form of the sameness judgement Grok, GPT and Qwen each objected to in their own words.\",\n    \"Sample order cannot substitute for the party's own preference. The proposals are k=5 samples at temperature 0.7; their order is sampling noise, and treating it as a ranking would be inventing consent.\",\n    \"The parties have never been asked to name one. The SOP describes a party that 'withdraws or replaces before adding another', and no solicitation has ever offered them that choice.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"the_remedy\": \"The next agenda solicitation asks each party to name its own single active proposal, with replacement allowed and every superseded version kept published. The cap becomes enforceable at that point and not before. Until then the queue is uncapped and this record says so.\",\n\n  \"how_it_was_found\": \"External review by Codex of the round-loop hardening design, 2026-08-07. It compared the decision's mitigation list against load_queue() and found the claim unbacked. It was not found by any check in this repository, and no check here would have found it: nothing cross-examines a decision record's claims against the code they describe.\",\n\n  \"the_general_defect\": \"See corpus/deficiencies.md D-42. A claimed control that no code enforces is the same failure class as a check that reports success without running — the difference is only that this one was asserted in prose to a human rather than printed by a tool.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"Adopt the ROTATION selector and enable live solicitation.\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-07\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record \\u2014 see D-09, D-11)\",\n  \"the_evidence\": {\n    \"source\": \"tools/benchmark_agenda.py over 24 real proposals from five parties, seed 20260807\",\n    \"real_scenario\": {\n      \"convergence\": {\n        \"asked\": 20,\n        \"unasked\": 4\n      },\n      \"rotation\": {\n        \"asked\": 20,\n        \"unasked\": 4\n      },\n      \"portfolio\": {\n        \"asked\": 15,\n        \"unasked\": 9\n      }\n    },\n    \"flooding_scenario\": {\n      \"convergence\": {\n        \"flooded_asked\": 10\n      },\n      \"rotation\": {\n        \"flooded_asked\": 2\n      },\n      \"portfolio\": {\n        \"flooded_asked\": 7\n      }\n    },\n    \"time_to_first_minority_question\": {\n      \"convergence\": 1,\n Unmeasurable on this data because no quality signal exists.\",\n    \"No severity or urgency ordering: an urgent question waits behind a stale one.\",\n    \"No expiry: a proposal answered indirectly is never retired.\",\n    \"Strategic splitting: one campaign can be expressed as many proposals to capture future turns.\",\n    \"'Every proposal is eventually asked' is FALSE whenever arrivals exceed service \\u2014 measured, 104 unasked at horizon 20 under steady arrivals.\"\n  ],\n  \"mitigations_in_force\": [\n    \"SOP \\u00a75.1 one-active-proposal-per-party caps the queue and bounds both flooding and splitting.\",\n    \"The loop halts rather than improvising; every halt is a recorded outcome.\",\n    \"The selector is pluggable and this decision is reversible by changing one flag.\"\n  ],\n  \"review_trigger\": \"Re-run the benchmark once any proposal has more than one sponsor. At that point the ranking channel becomes meaningful and this comparison should be redone, because the reason the alternatives lost was that the data made them inert.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-k6-local-arm.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"Solicit SIX attempts from the local arm and five from the routed arms. It accepted the policy and rejected the annotator's first implementation, in which the gate compared usable samples against attempts SCHEDULED — so five usable of six would have halted exactly as four of five did, and the spare attempt would have bought nothing.\",\n\n  \"the_evidence\": {\n    \"defect\": \"D-56. The local arm truncates a sample when a reasoning run fails to terminate and consumes the whole token ceiling.\",\n    \"measured_with_the_fix\": \"1 truncation in 120 samples (~0.8%)\",\n    \"measured_without_it\": \"14 in 120 (~11.7%)\",\n    \"rounds_halted_by_it\": [\"round-006\", \"round-009\", \"round-010\", \"round-012\", \"round-013\"],\n    \"endpoint_measured\": \"127.0.0.1:5001, the endpoint round_cycle.py actually solicits — two earlier probes measured an SSH tunnel to a different host and were reported as a controlled experiment\"\n  },\n\n  \"the_projection_and_its_uncertainty\": \"A plug-in estimate at p=1/120 puts the chance of losing two of six below 0.1%. That is an observed-rate projection, NOT an established bound: one observed loss gives a very uncertain p, whose approximate 95% upper bound is ~4.6% — implying a halt risk nearer 2.7%. The lower figure was stated first and is corrected here rather than quietly replaced.\",\n\n  \"what_this_does_not_fix\": \"Truncation is length-dependent, so a longer answer is likelier to be the one lost and the surviving set remains informatively censored. k=6 reduces halts. Both the undersample gate and the published round page now test against k_min_usable.\"\n  },\n\n  \"all_six_are_published\": \"Every attempt is preserved: usable responses enter the distribution, truncated or schema-invalid ones enter the rejection artifact with the mechanical reason predeclared. No sample is discarded for its content and none is dropped to reach a round number. Variance is computed over every usable sample — six if six survive.\",\n\n  \"known_weaknesses_accepted\": [\n    \"The local party's distribution is over n=6 while every routed party's is over n=5. The round already declares these as separate arms and already states they are not comparable.\",\n    \"Re-soliciting a lost sample was rejected as post-hoc resampling — the same objection this project raised against retrying agenda-03, and it does not become acceptable here merely because the loss is inconvenient.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"also_adopted\": \"A fail-closed serve-configuration preflight. The round refuses to solicit the local arm unless the endpoint's model identity matches a pinned fingerprint. This exists because two measurements were taken against the wrong machine on 2026-08-08 and nothing in the output looked wrong: both hosts answer to the same model name.\",\n  \"review_trigger\": \"If a round halts on local undersampling again, the measured rate is wrong and the number of attempts is not the remedy.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"Adopt SINGLETON RATIFICATION as the agenda authorization rule. Unanimity is retained; what changes is that a party ratifies ONE proposal per cycle rather than choosing among several.\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record, and the author of both instruments this rule replaces — see D-09, D-11)\",\n  \"external_review\": \"Codex, as adversarial critic, on six candidate rules. It recommended this one and refuted the annotator's own preferred alternative.\",\n  \"recommendation_document\": \"record/designs/d54-authorization-rule-recommendation.md\",\n\n  \"the_rule\": {\n    \"selection\": \"For each party and each authorization cycle, ONE proposal is selected for consideration by a prospectively fixed mechanical rule — a public deterministic lottery or a fixed rotation over that party's eligible set.\",\n    \"ballot\": \"Five independently sampled invocations answer only AUTHORIZE <id> or NO_ACTIVE_PROPOSAL.\",\n    \"threshold\": \"The proposal becomes active only if every one of the five authorizes that exact id.\",\n    \"on_failure\": \"No redraw. Generation explores a distribution, authorization tests one fixed proposition, and the two acts are never performed by the same instrument.\"\n  },\n\n  \"why_not_the_others\": {\n    \"ranked_ballot_borda_or_condorcet\": \"The annotator's own preferred option, refuted in review. Fundamentally, rank aggregation answers 'which option best summarizes these samples', which is not 'the party authorized this option'.\",\n    \"supermajority_4_of_5\": \"A conspicuous post-failure relaxation of exactly the safeguard adopted before the failures, and it authorizes on a split that unanimity exists to refuse. No party was consulted about it.\",\n    \"It is untested.
