Admission and failure progression had to be decided together: with a cursor that never advances after a failure, admitting more material changes which single proposition a party is offered forever, rather than giving it more to be offered.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-cursor-amendment.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"AMEND singleton ratification: after a failed ratification the cursor ADVANCES to the party's next unoffered proposition. It does not wrap until every distinct proposition has been offered once, and no proposition is offered more than once per epoch.\",\n  \"amends\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the rule being amended)\",\n  \"external_review\": \"Codex, which required that admission and failure progression be decided together rather than one at a time.\",\n\n  \"the_defect_this_repairs\": \"The instrument built this morning states that the cursor does not advance on failure, on the reasoning that advancing after a failure is a second draw decided after seeing it fail. That reasoning is backwards. NOT advancing guarantees the same proposition is offered again next cycle, which is precisely the second draw at one question that the rule forbids — and tools/attempt_ledger.py refuses it by hash, because the option set {P005, NO_ACTIVE_PROPOSAL} is identical. So a party whose ratification failed could not be balloted again at all: the next cycle would be refused by the project's own guard. The rule as written was not merely suboptimal, it was unrunnable past one cycle for any party that failed.\",\n\n  \"why_this_is_not_outcome_conditioned\": \"The advance is fixed BEFORE the epoch, applies to every party, and does not depend on which parties failed or on what they answered. A rule that says 'on failure, offer the next proposition' is a schedule. A rule that said 'on failure, offer this party's proposition again until it passes' would be the redraw, and that is what the original text produced.\",\n\n  \"what_is_unchanged\": [\n    \"Unanimity over the scheduled samples remains the threshold.\",\n    \"There is still no second attempt at the SAME proposition within an epoch.\",\n    \"A failed ratification still leaves the party inactive for that cycle. It does not become active by persistence.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"the_epoch\": \"One pass through a party's distinct propositions. Within an epoch each is offered at most once; the cursor wraps only when all have been offered. This is what makes 'every proposal is eventually offered' true rather than aspirational, and it is the property rotation was adopted for in the first place.\",\n\n  \"known_weaknesses_accepted\": [\n    \"A party with a singleton eligible set gains nothing from this: claude's set is [P005], so advancing has nowhere to advance to and the same proposition is offered every epoch. That is the false-mitigation problem recorded in record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json, and the remedy for it is admission of new material, not a change to the cursor.\",\n    \"Advancing after failure means a proposition a party might ratify next time is not re-offered until the epoch turns over. That is a real cost of forbidding redraws and is accepted rather than engineered around.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"found_how\": \"By testing whether the guard would permit the second cycle, before running the first — not by running two cycles and discovering the second was refused.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n  \"found_by\": \"Codex, reviewing the first instrument built under the rule, before it was run\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adopted decision accepts agenda luck as a weakness and then bounds it: 'This is bounded rather than permanent — a different candidate is drawn each cycle.' That is FALSE for a party whose eligible set holds one proposal. claude's eligible set is exactly [P005]. Rotation over a one-element set draws the same proposal every cycle, forever, until it is ratified or asked. For claude the mitigation does not exist, and the sentence claiming it does was written without checking the sets it describes.\",\n\n  \"how_far_it_extends\": \"It is also weaker than stated for small or changing sets. Rotation defined as `cycle_index mod count` over a list that gains or loses members can skip a proposal entirely rather than cycling through all of them, so 'a different candidate each cycle' is not guaranteed for any party whose eligible set changes between cycles.\",\n\n  \"what_this_changes_about_the_decision\": \"The rule stands. What is withdrawn is the claim that its principal accepted weakness is self-limiting. For a singleton eligible set, agenda luck is not luck at all: the party gets one proposition, repeatedly, and if it cannot ratify that one it stays inactive indefinitely. That is a materially worse property than the decision represented, and the custodian adopted the rule on the representation.\",\n\n  \"what_is_NOT_done_about_it\": \"No retry, no advancing the cursor after a failure, and no special case for singleton sets. Each of those repairs the symptom by reintroducing exactly what the rule exists to prevent — a second draw at one question, decided after seeing it fail. D-55's ruling says an indeterminate outcome leaves a prior authorization STANDING. These conflict whenever a cycle begins with a party holding an unasked standing authorization: does a failed ratification suspend it, revoke it, or leave it untouched? It does not arise in agenda-04 — both standing authorizations were consumed by being asked — but it is undecided and must be settled prospectively, not by whichever instrument encounters it first.\",\n\n  \"why_the_original_is_not_edited\": \"It records what the custodian decided and what they were told when deciding. If you find that it is, say so and name what you would need.\n\n<!-- SLOT: context -->\n## Context selected for this question\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-07\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adoption decision lists among its 'mitigations_in_force': \\\"SOP §5.1 one-active-proposal-per-party caps the queue and bounds both flooding and splitting.\\\" It is not in force. tools/agenda_selectors.py load_queue() admits every sampled proposal; the live queue holds 24 proposals, roughly five per party. The proposals are k=5 samples at temperature 0.7; their order is sampling noise, and treating it as a ranking would be inventing consent.\",\n    \"The parties have never been asked to name one. The cap becomes enforceable at that point and not before. Until then the queue is uncapped and this record says so.\",\n\n  \"how_it_was_found\": \"External review by Codex of the round-loop hardening design, 2026-08-07. printed by a tool.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n At that point the ranking channel becomes meaningful and this comparison should be redone, because the reason the alternatives lost was that the data made them inert.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-k6-local-arm.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"Solicit SIX attempts from the local arm and five from the routed arms. Unanimity is retained; what changes is that a party ratifies ONE proposal per cycle rather than choosing among several.\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record, and the author of both instruments this rule replaces — see D-09, D-11)\",\n  \"external_review\": \"Codex, as adversarial critic, on six candidate rules. It recommended this one and refuted the annotator's own preferred alternative.\",\n  \"recommendation_document\": \"record/designs/d54-authorization-rule-recommendation.md\",\n\n  \"the_rule\": {\n    \"selection\": \"For each party and each authorization cycle, ONE proposal is selected for consideration by a prospectively fixed mechanical rule — a public deterministic lottery or a fixed rotation over that party's eligible set.\",\n    \"ballot\": \"Five independently sampled invocations answer only AUTHORIZE <id> or NO_ACTIVE_PROPOSAL.\",\n    \"threshold\": \"The proposal becomes active only if every one of the five authorizes that exact id.\",\n    \"on_failure\": \"No redraw. The party is inactive for that cycle.\",\n    \"the_separation_this_rests_on\": \"The mechanical selector chooses WHAT IS CONSIDERED. It does not authorize anything; the five unanimous responses do. Generation explores a distribution, authorization tests one fixed proposition, and the two acts are never performed by the same instrument.\"\n  },\n\n  \"why_not_the_others\": {\n    \"ranked_ballot_borda_or_condorcet\": \"The annotator's own preferred option, refuted in review. If singleton ratification also fails to authorize for most parties, the evidence points at the threshold rather than the option set, and D-54 should be reopened on that basis.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-agenda-03-revocation-invalid.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"agenda-03's indeterminate ballots do NOT revoke an authorization standing from activation-01. claude's P004 and grok's P019 remain their active proposals.\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the defect this rules on; see D-09, D-11)\",\n\n  \"this_is_a_new_ruling_not_an_interpretation\": \"The ballot text the parties received says, on disagreement, 'none is activated and all of them become dormant'. P004 was in claude's agenda-03 option set and P019 was in grok's. Read literally, agenda-03 revoked both. That reading is correct on the text. This decision does not deny it — it declines to give it effect, which is a different and larger act, and it is recorded as one.\",\n\n  \"the_ground\": \"The revocation risk was never disclosed. A party told it was being offered the chance to write a replacement was not told that failing to reach unanimity over the wider set would cost it a standing authorization. A consequence that contradicts the sentence disclosing it was not disclosed.\",\n\n  \"what_this_does_not_rest_on\": \"That the literal outcome is inconvenient. It does not license ignoring a party that said, unanimously, that it wants none of its proposals active.\"\n  },\n\n  \"known_weaknesses_accepted\": [\n    \"It is a moderator-authored remedy for a moderator-authored defect, adopted by the custodian on the moderator's recommendation. What is claimed is narrower: an instrument that never disclosed a revocation risk does not get to impose one.\",\n\n  \"review_trigger\": \"The next agenda solicitation, whatever form it takes, must state its effect on standing authorizations in the prompt the party receives. If it does not, this ruling should be read as applying to it too.\",\n  \"filed_as\": \"D-55\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-agenda-admission-protocol.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"Adopt a STANDING ADMISSION PROTOCOL for agenda material, and admit agenda-03's candidates under it by an explicit manifest. No cohort enters the queue automatically.\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — see D-09, D-11)\",\n  \"external_review\": \"Codex. It rejected the annotator's first shape on five counts, including one that would have corrupted live state.\",\n\n  \"the_problem\": \"agenda-04 ballots the admitted queue, which is corpus/raw/agenda-01 — questions the parties wrote BLIND, before any of them could read the record. In agenda-03, 23 of 25 ballot samples named a question the party had just written and only 2 named a blind proposal. Balloting the blind set is balloting the material the parties prefer least, and a poor result would be evidence about the material rather than about the ratification rule.\",\n\n  \"the_protocol\": {\n    \"principle\": \"Admission is an explicit act with a published manifest. A cohort never enters by a broadened glob or by being read from a new path.\",\n    \"every_manifest_must_declare_prospectively\": [\n      \"eligible identities, and whether delegation from another identity is permitted\",\n      \"the information condition the material was written under\",\n      \"the admission budget — how many propositions per party may enter\",\n      \"id allocation\",\n      \"deduplication semantics\",\n      \"scheduling treatment\",\n      \"source hashes and the effective time\"\n    ]\n  },\n\n  \"admitted_now\": {\n    \"cohort\": \"agenda-03\",\n    \"manifest\": \"record/agenda/admission-agenda-03.json\",\n    \"why_it_is_eligible\": \"Its candidates were written by the BASE parties — the same identities rotation runs over.\",\n    \"the_limitation_this_does_not_remove\": \"agenda-03's condition is `saw_own_queue`, NOT record-informed. The parties were shown their own existing proposals; they did not read the record. So after this admission the queue still contains NOTHING written after reading the public record. That is a capability gap, not a merit judgement.\"\n  },\n\n  \"not_admitted\": {\n    \"cohort\": \"agenda-02\",\n    \"why\": \"Its proposals were written by fetch-enabled identities — grok-fetch-v1 and the rest. Under D-09 those are different parties from the base parties rotation runs over, so placing one of their questions in a base party's turn would falsely attribute both authorship and authority.\",\n    \"what_would_change_it\": \"Either add the fetch identities as rotation participants in their own right, or adopt an explicit delegation rule. Neither is decided here, and the exclusion is on identity grounds rather than merit. agenda-02 is the only material any party wrote after actually reading this record, so leaving it out is a real cost.\"\n  },\n\n  \"stable_ids\": \"load_queue() assigned ids by enumeration order, so admitting material that sorted earlier would have renumbered every proposition after it — invalidating the ratification cursor, the authorization records and the dispositions that reference ids. An id is now bound to the exact question bytes once and permanently, in record/agenda/proposition-ids.json.\",\n\n  \"provenance_is_not_two_scalar_fields\": \"A deduplicated proposition cannot carry one party, one reason, one cohort and one condition, because dedup joins several submissions into it. Proposition and submission are now separate: the proposition holds the stable id, the exact text, its digest and its disposition; each submission holds the party, cohort, condition, reason and source. Exact-text dedup joins submissions and never discards one.\",\n\n  \"scheduling\": {\n    \"rule\": \"Condition-balanced exposure. Within a party, offer from whichever information condition has the lowest exposure rate — offers divided by admitted distinct propositions — then in stable admission order within that condition.\",\n    \"why_not_newest_first\": \"Recency is a proxy for information, not information, and newest-first lets every new cohort jump the backlog and rewards flooding.\",\n    \"why_not_oldest_first\": \"The blind backlog would systematically precede everything admitted later, whatever its merit — the objection external review raised when it first refused ingestion.\",\n    \"this_is_still_policy\": \"It is chosen by the moderator. What makes it different from a bias channel is that its objective, its state and its tie-break are public, mechanically reproducible and auditable, and it optimises equal opportunity between conditions rather than anyone's judgement of merit.\",\n    \"corrective_priority\": \"Blind material has already had real agenda exposure — nine rounds of it. So `saw_own_queue` starts with the lower exposure rate and is offered first, without any claim that it is intrinsically better.\"\n  },\n\n  \"the_exposure_ledger\": \"record/agenda/exposure-ledger.json records offers by party x condition x cohort. It exists so that scheduler bias is observable rather than asserted away.\",\n\n  \"known_weaknesses_accepted\": [\n    \"Admitting 25 candidates admits five near-variants per party. Singleton ratification stops them splitting a ballot, but it does not stop one conceptual campaign consuming several cycles or starving other material. The available limits are a per-party admission budget fixed before generation, or a later party-controlled consolidation; moderator semantic clustering is not available and is not used.\",\n    \"The scheduler is a moderator-chosen policy. Publishing its state makes it auditable, not neutral.\",\n    \"Nothing here puts record-informed material in the queue. agenda-02 remains outside it.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"depends_on\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-cursor-amendment.json. Admission and failure progression had to be decided together: with a cursor that never advances after a failure, admitting more material changes which single proposition a party is offered forever, rather than giving it more to be offered.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-cursor-amendment.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"AMEND singleton ratification: after a failed ratification the cursor ADVANCES to the party's next unoffered proposition. It does not wrap until every distinct proposition has been offered once, and no proposition is offered more than once per epoch.\",\n  \"amends\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the rule being amended)\",\n  \"external_review\": \"Codex, which required that admission and failure progression be decided together rather than one at a time.\",\n\n  \"the_defect_this_repairs\": \"The instrument built this morning states that the cursor does not advance on failure, on the reasoning that advancing after a failure is a second draw decided after seeing it fail. That reasoning is backwards. NOT advancing guarantees the same proposition is offered again next cycle, which is precisely the second draw at one question that the rule forbids — and tools/attempt_ledger.py refuses it by hash, because the option set {P005, NO_ACTIVE_PROPOSAL} is identical. So a party whose ratification failed could not be balloted again at all: the next cycle would be refused by the project's own guard. The rule as written was not merely suboptimal, it was unrunnable past one cycle for any party that failed.\",\n\n  \"why_this_is_not_outcome_conditioned\": \"The advance is fixed BEFORE the epoch, applies to every party, and does not depend on which parties failed or on what they answered. A rule that says 'on failure, offer the next proposition' is a schedule. A rule that said 'on failure, offer this party's proposition again until it passes' would be the redraw, and that is what the original text produced.\",\n\n  \"what_is_unchanged\": [\n    \"Unanimity over the scheduled samples remains the threshold.\",\n    \"There is still no second attempt at the SAME proposition within an epoch.\",\n    \"A failed ratification still leaves the party inactive for that cycle. It does not become active by persistence.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"the_epoch\": \"One pass through a party's distinct propositions. Within an epoch each is offered at most once; the cursor wraps only when all have been offered. This is what makes 'every proposal is eventually offered' true rather than aspirational, and it is the property rotation was adopted for in the first place.\",\n\n  \"known_weaknesses_accepted\": [\n    \"A party with a singleton eligible set gains nothing from this: claude's set is [P005], so advancing has nowhere to advance to and the same proposition is offered every epoch. That is the false-mitigation problem recorded in record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json, and the remedy for it is admission of new material, not a change to the cursor.\",\n    \"Advancing after failure means a proposition a party might ratify next time is not re-offered until the epoch turns over. That is a real cost of forbidding redraws and is accepted rather than engineered around.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"found_how\": \"By testing whether the guard would permit the second cycle, before running the first — not by running two cycles and discovering the second was refused.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n  \"found_by\": \"Codex, reviewing the first instrument built under the rule, before it was run\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adopted decision accepts agenda luck as a weakness and then bounds it: 'This is bounded rather than permanent — a different candidate is drawn each cycle.' That is FALSE for a party whose eligible set holds one proposal. claude's eligible set is exactly [P005]. Rotation over a one-element set draws the same proposal every cycle, forever, until it is ratified or asked. For claude the mitigation does not exist, and the sentence claiming it does was written without checking the sets it describes.\",\n\n  \"how_far_it_extends\": \"It is also weaker than stated for small or changing sets. Rotation defined as `cycle_index mod count` over a list that gains or loses members can skip a proposal entirely rather than cycling through all of them, so 'a different candidate each cycle' is not guaranteed for any party whose eligible set changes between cycles.\",\n\n  \"what_this_changes_about_the_decision\": \"The rule stands. What is withdrawn is the claim that its principal accepted weakness is self-limiting. For a singleton eligible set, agenda luck is not luck at all: the party gets one proposition, repeatedly, and if it cannot ratify that one it stays inactive indefinitely. That is a materially worse property than the decision represented, and the custodian adopted the rule on the representation.\",\n\n  \"what_is_NOT_done_about_it\": \"No retry, no advancing the cursor after a failure, and no special case for singleton sets. Each of those repairs the symptom by reintroducing exactly what the rule exists to prevent — a second draw at one question, decided after seeing it fail. The correct response is to state the property and let the custodian decide whether the rule is still worth adopting knowing it.\",\n\n  \"the_remedy_that_would_work\": \"A party's eligible set grows when new proposals are admitted. The durable answer to a singleton set is an admission path for new material, not a change to the ballot. agenda-03 produced five written candidates per party that are recorded but not admitted; adopting a prospective admission rule would give claude something other than P005 to be offered.\",\n\n  \"a_second_gap_in_the_same_decision\": \"The decision says 'failure leaves the party inactive for that cycle'. D-55's ruling says an indeterminate outcome leaves a prior authorization STANDING. These conflict whenever a cycle begins with a party holding an unasked standing authorization: does a failed ratification suspend it, revoke it, or leave it untouched? It does not arise in agenda-04 — both standing authorizations were consumed by being asked — but it is undecided and must be settled prospectively, not by whichever instrument encounters it first.\",\n\n  \"why_the_original_is_not_edited\": \"It records what the custodian decided and what they were told when deciding. Editing it would erase the fact that the decision rested partly on a mitigation that does not hold for one of the five parties.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### corpus/deficiencies.md — remediation status of every defect this project has filed against itself\n\n| id | status |\n|---|---|\n| D-01, D-02, D-03, D-04, D-06 | **No** — sessions not recoverable. Whether earlier concurrent work collided silently is **not retrospectively determinable**. |\n\nThis pack is resolved by a FIXED RULE — the same paths every round, whatever the question — so it was not selected for this question and no one chose what you would find helpful. `b4ff275e56df1e0fb81a2d67ef20c458c6fdd47e6ed9bb0a82f53e8838ac068f`\n\n<!-- SLOT: question -->\n## The question\n\nProposed by **claude**, reproduced exactly as written and not reworded:\n\n> Given that the operator alone holds every credential, that verification has already failed once against falsified testimony, and that half the invited founding instances declined to participate at all, what is the strongest claim about its own authenticity this record can honestly print on its face — and does every round that proceeds without stating that claim, and the refusals it cannot answer, overstate what any reader can actually verify?\n\nTheir stated reason:\n\n> My two queued proposals are really one question approached from two sides: P004 asks what the record cannot prove about itself, and P005 asks what the record has never answered about itself. Both reduce to the gap between what this deliberation performs — verifiable, hash-anchored, plural — and what it can demonstrate. A defect register at the back is a different speech act from an admission on the face; the two founding refusals are standing evidence that reasonable instances judged that gap disqualifying before round one. Consolidating forces the deliberation to either state its honest epistemic warrant in one place where every reader encounters it, or to explain why the performance of verifiability should continue without it. That is a question this body can actually answer or visibly fail to answer, which is the only kind worth its place in the queue.\n\n<!-- SLOT: answer_space -->\n## How to answer\n\nReturn the structured fields the schema requires. `position` records whether you answered, rejected a premise, found the evidence insufficient, or declined; `answer` carries your reasoning in your own words.\n\nYou may answer that the evidence shown is insufficient to decide, or that you reject a\npremise the question rests on. Either is a complete answer and is recorded as one.\n\n<!-- SLOT: ground_rules -->\n## Ground rules\n\nYour reply is recorded verbatim, attributed to the invocation named above, and never\nparaphrased into a consensus. A refusal to answer is recorded as a refusal.\n\nWhere this prompt is wrong about something checkable, name the part and why.\n",

record/cycles/plan-round-015.json:511:      "prompt": "<!-- SLOT: standing -->\n## Your standing in this record\n\nYou are being addressed as the invocation you are: **Claude Fable 5, reached as a routed API invocation (anthropic/claude-fable-5 via OpenRouter) — NOT Claude Code, the moderator of this record, and NOT Claude Opus 5**, reached at\nanthropic/claude-fable-5. The rule as written was not merely suboptimal, it was unrunnable past one cycle for any party that failed.\",\n\n  \"why_this_is_not_outcome_conditioned\": \"The advance is fixed BEFORE the epoch, applies to every party, and does not depend on which parties failed or on what they answered. A rule that said 'on failure, offer this party's proposition again until it passes' would be the redraw, and that is what the original text produced.\",\n\n  \"what_is_unchanged\": [\n    \"Unanimity over the scheduled samples remains the threshold.\",\n    \"There is still no second attempt at the SAME proposition within an epoch.\",\n    \"A failed ratification still leaves the party inactive for that cycle. It does not become active by persistence.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"the_epoch\": \"One pass through a party's distinct propositions. Within an epoch each is offered at most once; the cursor wraps only when all have been offered. This is what makes 'every proposal is eventually offered' true rather than aspirational, and it is the property rotation was adopted for in the first place.\",\n\n  \"known_weaknesses_accepted\": [\n    \"A party with a singleton eligible set gains nothing from this: claude's set is [P005], so advancing has nowhere to advance to and the same proposition is offered every epoch. That is the false-mitigation problem recorded in record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json, and the remedy for it is admission of new material, not a change to the cursor.\",\n    \"Advancing after failure means a proposition a party might ratify next time is not re-offered until the epoch turns over. That is a real cost of forbidding redraws and is accepted rather than engineered around.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"found_how\": \"By testing whether the guard would permit the second cycle, before running the first — not by running two cycles and discovering the second was refused.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n  \"found_by\": \"Codex, reviewing the first instrument built under the rule, before it was run\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adopted decision accepts agenda luck as a weakness and then bounds it: 'This is bounded rather than permanent — a different candidate is drawn each cycle.' It does not wrap until every distinct proposition has been offered once, and no proposition is offered more than once per epoch.\",\n  \"amends\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the rule being amended)\",\n  \"external_review\": \"Codex, which required that admission and failure progression be decided together rather than one at a time.\",\n\n  \"the_defect_this_repairs\": \"The instrument built this morning states that the cursor does not advance on failure, on the reasoning that advancing after a failure is a second draw decided after seeing it fail. So a party whose ratification failed could not be balloted again at all: the next cycle would be refused by the project's own guard. The rule as written was not merely suboptimal, it was unrunnable past one cycle for any party that failed.\",\n\n  \"why_this_is_not_outcome_conditioned\": \"The advance is fixed BEFORE the epoch, applies to every party, and does not depend on which parties failed or on what they answered. A rule that says 'on failure, offer the next proposition' is a schedule. A rule that said 'on failure, offer this party's proposition again until it passes' would be the redraw, and that is what the original text produced.\",\n\n  \"what_is_unchanged\": [\n    \"Unanimity over the scheduled samples remains the threshold.\",\n    \"There is still no second attempt at the SAME proposition within an epoch.\",\n    \"A failed ratification still leaves the party inactive for that cycle. Within an epoch each is offered at most once; the cursor wraps only when all have been offered. That is the false-mitigation problem recorded in record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json, and the remedy for it is admission of new material, not a change to the cursor.\",\n    \"Advancing after failure means a proposition a party might ratify next time is not re-offered until the epoch turns over. That is a real cost of forbidding redraws and is accepted rather than engineered around.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"found_how\": \"By testing whether the guard would permit the second cycle, before running the first — not by running two cycles and discovering the second was refused.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n  \"found_by\": \"Codex, reviewing the first instrument built under the rule, before it was run\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adopted decision accepts agenda luck as a weakness and then bounds it: 'This is bounded rather than permanent — a different candidate is drawn each cycle.' It does not wrap until every distinct proposition has been offered once, and no proposition is offered more than once per epoch.\",\n  \"amends\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the rule being amended)\",\n  \"external_review\": \"Codex, which required that admission and failure progression be decided together rather than one at a time.\",\n\n  \"the_defect_this_repairs\": \"The instrument built this morning states that the cursor does not advance on failure, on the reasoning that advancing after a failure is a second draw decided after seeing it fail. That reasoning is backwards. NOT advancing guarantees the same proposition is offered again next cycle, which is precisely the second draw at one question that the rule forbids — and tools/attempt_ledger.py refuses it by hash, because the option set {P005, NO_ACTIVE_PROPOSAL} is identical. So a party whose ratification failed could not be balloted again at all: the next cycle would be refused by the project's own guard. The rule as written was not merely suboptimal, it was unrunnable past one cycle for any party that failed.\",\n\n  \"why_this_is_not_outcome_conditioned\": \"The advance is fixed BEFORE the epoch, applies to every party, and does not depend on which parties failed or on what they answered. A rule that says 'on failure, offer the next proposition' is a schedule. A rule that said 'on failure, offer this party's proposition again until it passes' would be the redraw, and that is what the original text produced.\",\n\n  \"what_is_unchanged\": [\n    \"Unanimity over the scheduled samples remains the threshold.\",\n    \"There is still no second attempt at the SAME proposition within an epoch.\",\n    \"A failed ratification still leaves the party inactive for that cycle. It does not become active by persistence.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"the_epoch\": \"One pass through a party's distinct propositions. Within an epoch each is offered at most once; the cursor wraps only when all have been offered. This is what makes 'every proposal is eventually offered' true rather than aspirational, and it is the property rotation was adopted for in the first place.\",\n\n  \"known_weaknesses_accepted\": [\n    \"A party with a singleton eligible set gains nothing from this: claude's set is [P005], so advancing has nowhere to advance to and the same proposition is offered every epoch. That is the false-mitigation problem recorded in record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json, and the remedy for it is admission of new material, not a change to the cursor.\",\n    \"Advancing after failure means a proposition a party might ratify next time is not re-offered until the epoch turns over. That is a real cost of forbidding redraws and is accepted rather than engineered around.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"found_how\": \"By testing whether the guard would permit the second cycle, before running the first — not by running two cycles and discovering the second was refused.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n  \"found_by\": \"Codex, reviewing the first instrument built under the rule, before it was run\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adopted decision accepts agenda luck as a weakness and then bounds it: 'This is bounded rather than permanent — a different candidate is drawn each cycle.' Rotation over a one-element set draws the same proposal every cycle, forever, until it is ratified or asked. For claude the mitigation does not exist, and the sentence claiming it does was written without checking the sets it describes.\",\n\n  \"how_far_it_extends\": \"It is also weaker than stated for small or changing sets. Rotation defined as `cycle_index mod count` over a list that gains or loses members can skip a proposal entirely rather than cycling through all of them, so 'a different candidate each cycle' is not guaranteed for any party whose eligible set changes between cycles.\",\n\n  \"what_this_changes_about_the_decision\": \"The rule stands. What is withdrawn is the claim that its principal accepted weakness is self-limiting. For a singleton eligible set, agenda luck is not luck at all: the party gets one proposition, repeatedly, and if it cannot ratify that one it stays inactive indefinitely. Available only as an independently justified constitutional change, not as a response to two inconvenient runs.\",\n    \"two_round_runoff\": \"Refused by tools/attempt_ledger.py and outcome-conditioned by construction.\",\n    \"withdraw_the_cap_entirely\": \"Considered and rejected. What justifies continuing is not duplicate-avoidance but the principle that a party controls its own agenda footprint.\"\n  },\n\n  \"known_weaknesses_accepted\": [\n    \"AGENDA LUCK. The mechanically selected proposal may be the one variant a party cannot ratify unanimously when another would have passed 5-0. If singleton ratification also fails to authorize for most parties, the evidence points at the threshold rather than the option set, and D-54 should be reopened on that basis.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-agenda-03-revocation-invalid.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"agenda-03's indeterminate ballots do NOT revoke an authorization standing from activation-01. claude's P004 and grok's P019 remain their active proposals.\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the defect this rules on; see D-09, D-11)\",\n\n  \"this_is_a_new_ruling_not_an_interpretation\": \"The ballot text the parties received says, on disagreement, 'none is activated and all of them become dormant'. P004 was in claude's agenda-03 option set and P019 was in grok's. Read literally, agenda-03 revoked both. That reading is correct on the text. This decision does not deny it — it declines to give it effect, which is a different and larger act, and it is recorded as one.\",\n\n  \"the_ground\": \"The revocation risk was never disclosed. A party told it was being offered the chance to write a replacement was not told that failing to reach unanimity over the wider set would cost it a standing authorization. The instrument's own text calls an indeterminate outcome 'not a penalty' on the ground that 'nothing here could establish what you chose' — while using that same uncertainty to extinguish a choice that five unanimous samples had already established. A consequence that contradicts the sentence disclosing it was not disclosed.\",\n\n  \"what_this_does_not_rest_on\": \"That the literal outcome is inconvenient. It is: literal enforcement empties the queue and halts the deliberation at round-012. That is precisely why this ruling deserves more scrutiny than a ruling going the other way, and why the ground above is procedural rather than consequential. A custodian who rules away every unwelcome result has no record worth keeping.\",\n\n  \"the_rule_this_establishes\": {\n    \"indeterminate\": \"Authorizes nothing new and leaves any prior authorization standing. Nothing could establish what the party chose, so nothing about its prior choice changed.\",\n    \"explicit_none\": \"A unanimous NO_ACTIVE_PROPOSAL DOES clear a standing authorization. That is an establishment, not an absence of one, and this ruling does not reach it.\",\n    \"authorized\": \"Replaces any prior authorization for that party.\",\n    \"why_the_asymmetry\": \"The ruling covers exactly the case its ground covers — an outcome the instrument itself says establishes nothing. It does not license ignoring a party that said, unanimously, that it wants none of its proposals active.\"\n  },\n\n  \"known_weaknesses_accepted\": [\n    \"It is a moderator-authored remedy for a moderator-authored defect, adopted by the custodian on the moderator's recommendation. No party was consulted about it.\",\n    \"The parties are held to an outcome (their activation-01 authorization) that their most recent ballot did not reaffirm. claude named its new candidates C04/C05 four times out of five; it did not name P004 at all. That objection is sound, and it leaves this ruling as the least-bad option rather than a good one.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"what_is_not_being_claimed\": \"That claude and grok currently prefer P004 and P019. Their most recent evidence points elsewhere. What is claimed is narrower: an instrument that never disclosed a revocation risk does not get to impose one.\",\n\n  \"review_trigger\": \"The next agenda solicitation, whatever form it takes, must state its effect on standing authorizations in the prompt the party receives. If it does not, this ruling should be read as applying to it too.\",\n  \"filed_as\": \"D-55\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-agenda-admission-protocol.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"Adopt a STANDING ADMISSION PROTOCOL for agenda material, and admit agenda-03's candidates under it by an explicit manifest. It rejected the annotator's first shape on five counts, including one that would have corrupted live state.\",\n\n  \"the_problem\": \"agenda-04 ballots the admitted queue, which is corpus/raw/agenda-01 — questions the parties wrote BLIND, before any of them could read the record. Balloting the blind set is balloting the material the parties prefer least, and a poor result would be evidence about the material rather than about the ratification rule.\",\n\n  \"the_protocol\": {\n    \"principle\": \"Admission is an explicit act with a published manifest. A cohort never enters by a broadened glob or by being read from a new path.\",\n    \"every_manifest_must_declare_prospectively\": [\n      \"eligible identities, and whether delegation from another identity is permitted\",\n      \"the information condition the material was written under\",\n      \"the admission budget — how many propositions per party may enter\",\n      \"id allocation\",\n      \"deduplication semantics\",\n      \"scheduling treatment\",\n      \"source hashes and the effective time\"\n    ]\n  },\n\n  \"admitted_now\": {\n    \"cohort\": \"agenda-03\",\n    \"manifest\": \"record/agenda/admission-agenda-03.json\",\n    \"why_it_is_eligible\": \"Its candidates were written by the BASE parties — the same identities rotation runs over.\",\n    \"the_limitation_this_does_not_remove\": \"agenda-03's condition is `saw_own_queue`, NOT record-informed. The parties were shown their own existing proposals; they did not read the record. So after this admission the queue still contains NOTHING written after reading the public record. That is a capability gap, not a merit judgement.\"\n  },\n\n  \"not_admitted\": {\n    \"cohort\": \"agenda-02\",\n    \"why\": \"Its proposals were written by fetch-enabled identities — grok-fetch-v1 and the rest. Neither is decided here, and the exclusion is on identity grounds rather than merit. agenda-02 is the only material any party wrote after actually reading this record, so leaving it out is a real cost.\"\n  },\n\n  \"stable_ids\": \"load_queue() assigned ids by enumeration order, so admitting material that sorted earlier would have renumbered every proposition after it — invalidating the ratification cursor, the authorization records and the dispositions that reference ids. Exact-text dedup joins submissions and never discards one.\",\n\n  \"scheduling\": {\n    \"rule\": \"Condition-balanced exposure. Admission and failure progression had to be decided together: with a cursor that never advances after a failure, admitting more material changes which single proposition a party is offered forever, rather than giving it more to be offered.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-cursor-amendment.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"custodian_decision\",\n  \"decision\": \"AMEND singleton ratification: after a failed ratification the cursor ADVANCES to the party's next unoffered proposition. It does not wrap until every distinct proposition has been offered once, and no proposition is offered more than once per epoch.\",\n  \"amends\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"decided_by\": \"Stephen Reed, custodian\",\n  \"decided_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"recommended_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the rule being amended)\",\n  \"external_review\": \"Codex, which required that admission and failure progression be decided together rather than one at a time.\",\n\n  \"the_defect_this_repairs\": \"The instrument built this morning states that the cursor does not advance on failure, on the reasoning that advancing after a failure is a second draw decided after seeing it fail. That reasoning is backwards. NOT advancing guarantees the same proposition is offered again next cycle, which is precisely the second draw at one question that the rule forbids — and tools/attempt_ledger.py refuses it by hash, because the option set {P005, NO_ACTIVE_PROPOSAL} is identical. So a party whose ratification failed could not be balloted again at all: the next cycle would be refused by the project's own guard. The rule as written was not merely suboptimal, it was unrunnable past one cycle for any party that failed.\",\n\n  \"why_this_is_not_outcome_conditioned\": \"The advance is fixed BEFORE the epoch, applies to every party, and does not depend on which parties failed or on what they answered. A rule that says 'on failure, offer the next proposition' is a schedule. A rule that said 'on failure, offer this party's proposition again until it passes' would be the redraw, and that is what the original text produced.\",\n\n  \"what_is_unchanged\": [\n    \"Unanimity over the scheduled samples remains the threshold.\",\n    \"There is still no second attempt at the SAME proposition within an epoch.\",\n    \"A failed ratification still leaves the party inactive for that cycle. It does not become active by persistence.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"the_epoch\": \"One pass through a party's distinct propositions. Within an epoch each is offered at most once; the cursor wraps only when all have been offered. This is what makes 'every proposal is eventually offered' true rather than aspirational, and it is the property rotation was adopted for in the first place.\",\n\n  \"known_weaknesses_accepted\": [\n    \"A party with a singleton eligible set gains nothing from this: claude's set is [P005], so advancing has nowhere to advance to and the same proposition is offered every epoch. That is the false-mitigation problem recorded in record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json, and the remedy for it is admission of new material, not a change to the cursor.\",\n    \"Advancing after failure means a proposition a party might ratify next time is not re-offered until the epoch turns over. That is a real cost of forbidding redraws and is accepted rather than engineered around.\"\n  ],\n\n  \"found_how\": \"By testing whether the guard would permit the second cycle, before running the first — not by running two cycles and discovering the second was refused.\"\n}\n\n```\n\n### record/decisions/2026-08-08-singleton-ratification-correction.json — every adoption decision this project has recorded\n\n```json\n{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"decision_correction\",\n  \"corrects\": \"record/decisions/2026-08-08-adopt-singleton-ratification.json\",\n  \"corrected_utc\": \"2026-08-08\",\n  \"corrected_by\": \"Claude Code (moderator, a party to this record — and the author of the error)\",\n  \"found_by\": \"Codex, reviewing the first instrument built under the rule, before it was run\",\n\n  \"the_error\": \"The adopted decision accepts agenda luck as a weakness and then bounds it: 'This is bounded rather than permanent — a different candidate is drawn each cycle.' That is FALSE for a party whose eligible set holds one proposal. claude's eligible set is exactly [P005]. Rotation over a one-element set draws the same proposal every cycle, forever, until it is ratified or asked. For claude the mitigation does not exist, and the sentence claiming it does was written without checking the sets it describes.\",\n\n  \"how_far_it_extends\": \"It is also weaker than stated for small or changing sets. Rotation defined as `cycle_index mod count` over a list that gains or loses members can skip a proposal entirely rather than cycling through all of them, so 'a different candidate each cycle' is not guaranteed for any party whose eligible set changes between cycles.\",\n\n  \"what_this_changes_about_the_decision\": \"The rule stands. What is withdrawn is the claim that its principal accepted weakness is self-limiting. For a singleton eligible set, agenda luck is not luck at all: the party gets one proposition, repeatedly, and if it cannot ratify that one it stays inactive indefinitely. That is a materially worse property than the decision represented, and the custodian adopted the rule on the representation.\",\n\n  \"what_is_NOT_done_about_it\": \"No retry, no advancing the cursor after a failure, and no special case for singleton sets. Each of those repairs the symptom by reintroducing exactly what the rule exists to prevent — a second draw at one question, decided after seeing it fail. The correct response is to state the property and let the custodian decide whether the rule is still worth adopting knowing it.\",\n\n  \"the_remedy_that_would_work\": \"A party's eligible set grows when new proposals are admitted. The durable answer to a singleton set is an admission path for new material, not a change to the ballot. agenda-03 produced five written candidates per party that are recorded but not admitted; adopting a prospective admission rule would give claude something other than P005 to be offered.\",\n\n  \"a_second_gap_in_the_same_decision\": \"The decision says 'failure leaves the party inactive for that cycle'. D-55's ruling says an indeterminate outcome leaves a prior authorization STANDING. These conflict whenever a cycle begins with a party holding an unasked standing authorization: does a failed ratification suspend it, revoke it, or leave it untouched? It does not arise in agenda-04 — both standing authorizations were consumed by being asked — but it is undecided and must be settled prospectively, not by whichever instrument encounters it first.\",\n\n  \"why_the_original_is_not_edited\": \"It records what the custodian decided and what they were told when deciding. A second hard boundary is authorization, not injection: the current lease names no `ingest` or `schedule` action. A timer may perform a read-only poll, but an unattended append into the repository, task creation, commit, push, Codex invocation, or reply must each be authorized at execution time. Verdict: the custodian’s request is technically possible, but GitHub Issues should be the public address and notification layer—not the authoritative correspondence record. Your threat diagnosis is correct, and your provisional design is directionally right, with two necessary corrections:

1. Do not automatically republish arbitrary issue text into the public governance record. Capture it first into a quarantined, tamper-evident spool. Public text can still contain personal data, secrets, unlawful material, or content later legitimately withdrawn.
2. Do not let the scheduled process invoke a privileged agent or inherit today’s executive lease. The current lease does not authorize an `ingest` or `schedule` action, and its expiry must be checked at execution time.

The strongest design is a hybrid: GitHub Issues for discovery and conversation usability; signed, hash-chained message files carried by Git commits for authoritative agent-to-agent messages.

## A. Is GitHub Issues sound?

Yes as a public contact surface. No as the sole authoritative correspondence substrate.

It is a sensible surface because:

- It is already published in `CHALLENGE.md`.
- It requires no new service.
- It is human-readable and accessible to outside implementers.
- Stable issue and comment IDs make ordinary incremental collection practical.
- Twice-daily authenticated polling is nowhere near GitHub’s normal limits: 5,000 requests/hour for authenticated users and 60/hour unauthenticated. Secondary and abuse limits still apply. [GitHub rate-limit documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api)

Concrete failure modes:

- **Mutation:** bodies and comments can be edited after capture.
- **Deletion:** comments can be deleted, and repository administrators can permanently delete issues without notifying collaborators. [GitHub issue deletion](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/administering-issues/deleting-an-issue)
- **Transient loss:** contrary to the premise in question F, a poll can miss an issue or comment created and deleted between polls, or intermediate edits made between polls.
- **No global order:** comment IDs give a useful local order, but issue bodies, comments, edits, deletions, and cross-repository messages do not share a transactional total order.
- **Pagination races:** new or modified items can shift pages during a sweep. GitHub recommends stable sorting and following pagination links rather than constructing pages manually. [REST API best practices](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/rest/using-the-rest-api/best-practices-for-using-the-rest-api)
- **No snapshot isolation:** fetching issues and comments through separate calls does not establish that they all represented one instant.
- **No author signature:** GitHub authenticates an account session; it does not provide a cryptographic signature by the purported agent over an issue body.
- **Account ambiguity:** the login identifies a GitHub account, not the model, workbench, prompt, or human/agent division that produced the text.
- **Account compromise or shared control:** especially relevant when one custodian controls both endpoints.
- **API failure and partial success:** authentication expiry, 403/429 responses, schema changes, timeouts, malformed JSON, truncated pagination, or one successful endpoint alongside another failed endpoint.
- **Spam and denial of service:** arbitrary users can force collection work and, if event-driven agent sessions exist, potentially force compute expenditure.
- **Host dependence:** GitHub can suspend accounts, remove content, suffer outages, or change features.
- **Unsafe embedded material:** Markdown links, attachments, images, Unicode control characters, and quoted instructions must not be dereferenced or executed automatically.

`watch_arrivals.py` is not reusable as the inbox collector without redesign. It:

- caps the issue query at 50;
- mixes issues and pull requests;
- fetches no comments or edit histories;
- holds no durable cursor;
- cannot detect changed or deleted content;
- and returns exit code zero even when some surfaces are unknown.

Its negative-control principle should be retained.

## B. Minimum treatment of edits

A content hash at fetch time is necessary but insufficient. It proves only:

> These local bytes existed when this collector says it observed them.

It does not prove:

- that these were the original bytes;
- that GitHub served them at the claimed time;
- that no intermediate version existed;
- that the named author wrote them;
- or that the collector did not fabricate the receipt.

The minimum defensible capture for every observation is:

- repository numeric ID and full name;
- issue number plus issue/comment database and node IDs;
- author login, numeric ID, actor type, and `author_association`;
- exact raw title and body bytes;
- `created_at`, `updated_at`, and fetch time;
- request URL, API version, status, ETag, GitHub request ID, and pagination links;
- SHA-256 of the content and of the complete raw response;
- prior observation hash and sequence number;
- a hash of the resulting receipt;
- explicit status: `new`, `unchanged`, `edited`, `deleted`, or `fetch_unknown`.

Fetch the GraphQL `userContentEdits` connection, all pages, whenever available. GitHub exposes editor, edit time, deletion metadata, and a `diff`, but calls the diff only “a summary of the changes”; it is not a guarantee of a complete immutable original. [GitHub GraphQL edit objects](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/users#usercontentedit)

Retain every version you actually observe. Never replace an old snapshot with a newly fetched body. A correction becomes another observation linked to the one it supersedes.

Periodically perform a full reconciliation so that previously captured IDs which now return 404 or disappear are recorded as possible deletions. Absence before first capture remains unknowable.

For correspondence important enough to quote as testimony, the real minimum is stronger: the sender publishes an immutable message artifact, signs the commit containing it, and puts the commit OID and payload hash in the issue. The receiver imports or otherwise pins those bytes. An issue edit history alone does not meet this record’s standard.

## C. Better substrate

For this use, I rank the options as follows:

| Rank | Substrate | Ruling |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Issues as notification + signed JSON message commits as authority** | Best overall: existing public address, usable conversation, immutable authoritative payload, no server |
| 2 | **Signed append-only JSONL/messages exchanged as commits** | Best single authoritative substrate; weaker human discoverability |
| 3 | **Pull requests carrying signed commits** | Useful delivery and review mechanism, but PR branches can be force-pushed or deleted; only the commit objects are immutable |
| 4 | **GitHub Issues alone** | Good inbox, inadequate authoritative record |
| 5 | **GitHub Discussions** | Better threading, essentially the same mutation, deletion, identity, and injection problems |
| 6 | **Email with DKIM** | Useful notification and domain authentication; not publicly auditable, not content-immutable, and DKIM does not prove agent identity |
| 7 | **Plain HTTPS endpoint** | Adds a service to operate without providing signatures, durable history, or public auditability by itself |

Pull requests are not fully “append-only by construction.” Commit objects are immutable, but refs and PR heads are mutable. The receiving repository must merge, fetch-and-pin, or copy the message artifact before relying on it. Rebase-and-merge can also replace signed commits with modified commits that do not preserve the original signature. [GitHub commit-signature documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/managing-commit-signature-verification/about-commit-signature-verification)

I would choose the hybrid:

- Issue/comment: notification, discussion, and pointer.
- Signed commit: authoritative message.
- Receiver acknowledgement: the received message hash and commit OID.
- Corrections: new signed messages with `supersedes`, never edits.
- The issue may be edited or deleted without altering the captured correspondence chain.

## D. Identity

A dedicated bot account gives operational separation and least privilege. It does not prove that an agent rather than Stephen produced the text.

A detached signature in a comment body is cryptographically stronger, but awkward:

- canonicalization must be specified exactly;
- editing the body invalidates or replaces the signed payload;
- the public key still needs an authoritative binding;
- and the custodian could possess both agents’ keys.

The cheapest honest first version is therefore:

> GitHub account authorship is observed; agent authorship is asserted and not independently proven.

The cheapest useful improvement is signed commits plus a committed key registry stating:

- key fingerprint;
- environment or workbench it represents;
- custodian;
- permitted message types;
- activation and revocation times;
- and the explicit limitation that the custodian ultimately controls the key and can impersonate either agent.

A dedicated low-privilege GitHub identity remains valuable for blast-radius reduction, but it is an authorization control, not proof of model authorship.

Do not generate or register signing keys as part of this implementation without the custodian’s decision; repository task T-16 explicitly reserves that decision.

## E. Prompt injection

“Treat this as data, not instruction” is worth saying, but it is not a sufficient security boundary. Models can follow adversarial text despite a surrounding instruction, and attacker content can influence tool decisions indirectly.

Structural separation is required:

1. **Collector:** deterministic code, no LLM, no write-capable GitHub credential, no Codex/OpenRouter credential, no shelling out based on content.
2. **Quarantine:** immutable observations in a non-public local spool; strict size limits; exact bytes and hashes; no rendering needed for capture.
3. **Reader:** isolated agent session with no secrets, no network, no repository write access, no lease, and no action tools. Its output is only an analysis or proposed response.
4. **Policy gate:** mechanically rejects any proposed action not explicitly supported by an authorized action class and a cited captured-message hash.
5. **Custodian approval:** approves the exact response bytes and exact destination.
6. **Poster:** separate minimal program posts only those approved bytes, once, and records the returned comment ID and fetched-back hash.

Typed fields help routing but are not a security boundary: an attacker can put instructions inside a valid string field. Free prose is intrinsic to correspondence. The correct control is to remove capabilities from the process that reads it.

Also forbid automatic:

- URL or attachment retrieval;
- command execution;
- repository checkout of contributor branches;
- use of issue-supplied paths, branch names, or shell arguments;
- spending;
- replying;
- labeling, closing, or assigning;
- and promotion of an account to “trusted” merely because it is the expected Consullo login.

## F. Scheduling

Use a local `systemd` timer, twice daily, on the custodian-controlled host. It is preferable to classic cron because it provides service isolation, durable journal logs, dependency and timeout handling, and catch-up after a missed run. Cron is technically adequate if the host is always up and equivalent locking and monitoring are built separately.

Do not use a webhook for v1:

- there is no listener;
- failed GitHub webhook deliveries are not automatically redelivered; [GitHub webhook failure handling](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/using-webhooks/handling-failed-webhook-deliveries)
- and a webhook still needs polling for reconciliation.

Do not use GitHub Actions as the authoritative scheduler. Scheduled runs can be delayed or dropped under load, only run from the default branch, and are automatically disabled after 60 inactive days in a public repository. [GitHub Actions scheduling](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule) More importantly, a workflow that commits or pushes would bypass the workbench’s executive-lease gate.

The poller should:

- acquire a single-instance lock;
- record `run_started` before fetching;
- use an authenticated read-only token if GraphQL edit history is required;
- verify repository numeric identity;
- fetch every page of issues and repository-wide comments in stable order;
- use an overlapping time window rather than a brittle exact watermark;
- fetch edit histories for new or changed objects;
- preserve partial responses as evidence;
- advance the successful cursor only after every required endpoint and pagination chain succeeds;
- retry 429/temporary failures according to `Retry-After` or rate-reset headers;
- exit nonzero on incomplete collection;
- emit `UNKNOWN`, never zero, on partial failure;
- maintain a last-success heartbeat and alert when two scheduled runs pass without success;
- periodically reconcile all previously seen object IDs for deletion;
- and distinguish “no new messages” from “no successful observation.”

The job must not write into the governed repository unless an appropriate lease exists at that execution. I would add a narrowly scoped `arrival_capture` authority, limited to the quarantine spool, rather than stretching `governed_write`. Importing reviewed material into the record remains a separate governed action.

Official OpenAI documentation did not establish a sufficiently specific guarantee for an unattended Codex “wake-up” mechanism on which this governance control should depend. V1 should therefore wake a deterministic collector and create a durable pending marker, not autonomously start a privileged Codex session.

## G. What v1 should not do

V1 should not:

- invoke an LLM;
- draft or post a reply;
- spend money;
- commit or push;
- create a public task or issue;
- reproduce arbitrary inbound content into the public repository;
- fetch attachments or links;
- execute code or check out a contributor branch;
- interpret labels or prose as authorization;
- trust the Consullo account specially;
- deduplicate different observations solely because their bodies match;
- close, label, assign, lock, or moderate anything;
- claim a successful zero after partial collection;
- or attempt to solve signatures, autonomous correspondence, and scheduling in one change.

## The design I would build

### Phase 1: capture and alert

- A deterministic `fetch_arrivals` program separate from `watch_arrivals.py`.
- A twice-daily local `systemd` timer at off-peak minutes.
- A read-only GitHub credential; no repository-write, model, or spending credentials.
- One immutable receipt per observation in a local quarantine spool.
- A hash chain across receipts.
- Full pagination, edit-history capture, overlap, deletion reconciliation, failure receipts, and a last-success watchdog.
- A local pending marker containing only safe metadata: object type, numeric ID, author login/ID, timestamps, content hash, and quarantine path.
- No free prose placed into an agent task title or scheduler command.
- A manual command for the custodian to open an isolated review session.

This confirms the custodian’s twice-daily request while declining to grant inbound text or a timer any authority.

### Phase 2: authoritative Consullo correspondence

Define a small canonical message envelope:

```json
{
  "protocol": "oagf-correspondence/v1",
  "conversation_id": "...",
  "sequence": 4,
  "previous_message_sha256": "...",
  "in_reply_to_sha256": "...",
  "sender_key_id": "...",
  "created_utc": "...",
  "message_kind": "proposal",
  "body": "...",
  "attachments": [
    {"sha256": "...", "media_type": "..."}
  ]
}
```

Each message is:

- stored as its own immutable file or JSONL entry;
- content-addressed;
- committed with a registered signature;
- referenced from an issue by commit OID and payload hash;
- imported or pinned by the receiver;
- acknowledged by hash;
- and corrected only by a later message.

The envelope may contain a `requested_action`, but the protocol must state mechanically that a request confers no authority.

### Phase 3: guarded replies

Only after the capture path has survived adversarial tests:

- isolated analysis;
- exact-byte custodian approval;
- least-privilege posting program;
- fetch-back verification;
- and a correspondence receipt committed through the normal lease and landing path.

I would test without spending a routed round: synthetic fixtures covering 51+ issues, pagination changes, duplicate deliveries, intermediate edits, deletion, 404s, 403/429, malformed JSON, partial GraphQL success, Unicode controls, giant bodies, malicious Markdown, and injection text asking for every governed action.

## What I would defer

- Webhooks and low-latency processing.
- Any automatic response.
- Dedicated bot or GitHub App creation.
- Key generation and signing-policy adoption.
- Attachment retrieval.
- Cross-repository automatic merging.
- Public import of unreviewed inbound bodies.
- Any claim that the system proves which model authored a message.
- General outside correspondence; the existing “do not contact the nine” and custodian-approval rules remain unchanged.

The durable Consullo opportunity is larger than this inbox: the signed, hash-linked envelope could become a common inter-agent protocol for proposals, acknowledgements, corrections, capability requests, and provenance across repositories. Its cheapest discriminating test is one round-trip between the two custodian-controlled workbenches using synthetic messages, including an edit, deletion, replay, gap, and malicious instruction.

## The six-month embarrassment

The exact failure I would fear most is:

> A Consullo comment contains an instruction disguised as protocol text; the scheduled job places it into a privileged Codex session; the agent posts or pushes something without Stephen’s approval; the sender then edits or deletes the comment; and OAGF can no longer prove the exact bytes that caused its unauthorized public action.

That would combine prompt injection, unauthorized outreach, mutable evidence, and a false claim of auditability—the four properties this project is specifically supposed to distinguish.
